## What the script does

One step: `write(ctx.loadRows)` — all 10 000 rows at the default point — into a
freshly built, empty binding whose two views are already subscribed, then
`settle()` (scenarios.ts:3091-3094). Each consumer must produce exactly one
distinct render and A a full window (scenarios.ts:3095-3102). The model starts
empty (scenarios.ts:3103-3109); the worker loads no opening state for a
`rebuild` script (worker.ts:362, 385-394).

## Representativeness

Hydrating a list from a fetch is something every list screen does, usually once
per navigation; 10 000 rows is large but realistic for an admin table or a
local-first cache. js-framework-benchmark's "create 1,000 / 10,000 rows" is the
same task measured with the DOM. The suite's version is stronger in demanding a
correct sorted, windowed view at the end and weaker in excluding parse, framework
and construction cost.

## The standing record, checked

`ORDINARY_SCRIPT` (scenarios.ts:86-169, listed at :97). Holds for this script.
WHY-EACH-ROW.md records two earlier explanations of this row ("batch insert —
oimdb is ~4× effector" and "batch insert — signaldb, figure retracted until
re-measured"); both were measured on earlier code and are not re-verified here,
and the signaldb figure is retracted because its wiring has since changed.

card.models: A page of new items arriving into a populated, newest-first list (a feed refresh, new orders, new messages) in one frame.
card.measures: Insert of genuinely new keys into a full store with fifty ordered groups and live subscriptions, and the re-derivation of every affected window.
favours: Stores with an ordered per-group index that can place a new row by binary search, over stores that rescan or re-sort the group.

For array-backed ordered buckets, arrival at position 0 is the most expensive splice position (all rows shift); for linked or tree-backed orders it is not special. The engine's ordered bucket inserts by `splice` (packages/core/src/engine/bucket/array/OIMBucketSlotsServiceArrayDriven.ts:154).
biases: Every new row ranks below every stored row (`rank: -(i + 1)`, dataset.ts:909-915), so each arrives at the HEAD of its group's window (scenarios.ts:3900-3903). Realistic for newest-first lists; it never asks for a mid-order insert, and it guarantees every window changes.
100 rows at the default point, two per group (`INSERT_COUNT`, dataset.ts:215). A modest page; a large page into a large store is asked by `growUnderSubscription`.
One `write(rows)` call (scenarios.ts:3932-3935): adapters can batch inside it; eager and deferred stores are on equal terms.

The untimed restore removes the rows (scenarios.ts:3928-3931), so the store never grows; a store whose removal leaves residue (tombstones, holes in arrays) is measured in its post-removal state on every sample after the first. Direction unverified.
card.summary: A realistic feed-style insert into a populated store; its newest-first ranks fix the arrival position at the head.
card.body:
## What the script does

One step: `write(ctx.insertRows)` (`INSERT_COUNT` = max(2·GROUPS, 2·WINDOW) = 100
rows with ids no stored row has, dataset.ts:215, 909-915; cloned once by the worker
as `insertRows`), then one `settle()` (scenarios.ts:3932-3935). `check`: view A holds
`min(WINDOW, groupSize + 2)` rows and view B a full window, view A's head is an
inserted row (`f` prefix), at least one delivery per view (scenarios.ts:3944-3956).
`finalStateOnly` (scenarios.ts:3921); `repeatable: false` (:3924).

## Representativeness

Inserting a page of new items into a list that already holds many is ordinary
(pagination, live feeds, "load newer"). Newest-first ordering is typical for feeds
and inboxes. js-framework-benchmark's "append 1,000 rows" is the opposite end of the
order (tail). This suite asks the head only.

## The standing record, checked

`ORDINARY_SCRIPT` (scenarios.ts:86-169, signed at :98). Holds for this script.

card.models: A feed or log that keeps receiving new items while it is on screen, so each batch lands in a store earlier batches already grew.
card.measures: The cost of inserting a batch of new keys as a function of how much the store already holds, with both views re-derived after every batch.
favours: Structures whose insert cost does not depend on where in the order the new key lands, or that sort lazily at derivation time.

Against array-backed ordered buckets that insert by shifting: every batch is ranked below everything already stored (dataset.ts:919-938), so every new row lands at position 0 of its group. That is the worst case for a shifting insert and the best case for nothing. Direction asserted from the shape, not measured.
biases: Every batch is visible: newest rows are ranked most negative (`rank: -(INSERT_COUNT + MOVER_COUNT + 1 + minted)`, dataset.ts:932), so each batch arrives at the head of all fifty windows and changes both views. An infinite list appends below the fold, where nothing re-derives; a chat or activity feed prepends a few rows per frame. This asks the prepend case at batch size.

Batch size is max(INSERT_COUNT, N/20) = 500 rows per frame at N = 10000 (dataset.ts:215, 248, 919-922), 10 per group per frame. Live feeds bring a handful per frame; 500 is a page load, eight times over.

Growth is bounded at 40 % over eight frames (GROWTH_FRAMES dataset.ts:235, GROWTH_FRACTION :248), as the description states (scenarios.ts:3973-3975). A cost that turns super-linear only at larger multiples is not reached.

The untimed `restore` drops and rebuilds the whole store every sample (scenarios.ts:3988-3993). Where the worker has `gc` exposed, `collect` runs it untimed before every timed sample (measure.ts:45-47, 73-74; worker.ts:63-67), so the discarded store is not collected inside the clock; without `gc` it may be. Whether a given run had `gc` is carried as `gcAvailable` in the result (worker.ts:64).
card.summary: A real growth pattern asked at its most visible and heaviest (500-row prepends to every group, eight times), so it prices ordered-insert cost at the head rather than typical feed growth.
card.body:
## What the script does

`GROWTH_FRAMES` = 8 steps (scenarios.ts:3981, 3994-3999): `write` of one prepared
batch of new keys, then `settle`. No row is removed between frames. Batches are
cloned once per process in `prepare` (:3985-3987). Each step is one binding call,
so the script does not use `frame`. `repeatable: false` (:3984).

## What decides correctness

`check` (scenarios.ts:4000-4008): both windows full, view A's head is a grown row
(`h` prefix, dataset.ts:930), and at least `GROWTH_FRAMES` DISTINCT renders per
view. Every frame changes both windows, so the distinct floor is the guard that
matches the script; the previous card's finding that `check` counted deliveries
(and so redundant ones) no longer holds. The description still says "at least one
delivery per frame" (:3979), which is weaker than what `check` asks.
`finalStateOnly` (:3983) compares the final state of both views with the model
(worker.ts:419-447), and the population and grouping audits read all 14000 rows
and fifty buckets afterwards (worker.ts:462-464). A store that dropped or
mis-ordered rows fails there.

## Representativeness

Stores that grow under a live subscription are common and every other script
runs at a fixed population, so the row fills a real gap. It is narrow because
it asks only head insertion at page-sized batches; the append-below-the-fold case,
which is the more frequent one for infinite lists, is not asked by any script.

## The standing record, checked

`ORDINARY_SCRIPT` (scenarios.ts:86-169, signed at :100). A1 holds through the head
check and the distinct floor. B4: both views change per step and the floor counts
one window delivery per step (floor.ts:76-87, 95), so the floor understates the
minimum, the safe direction.

card.models: A screen opening from nothing: create the store and its two views, subscribe, load every row, and deliver the first frame.
card.measures: Construction plus subscription plus bulk load plus first delivery, all inside the clock; read against `batchInsert` for the construction share.
favours: Libraries cheap to construct and to subscribe (no schema compilation, no per-view setup).
Libraries that do not render an empty frame at subscribe time, but only in the counters: the render count is not judged (`finalStateOnly`, scenarios.ts:4052-4067).
biases: It is not cold. The timing loop runs the whole construction at least once and up to `warmup` iterations before sampling (measure.ts:55-69; `planFor` warmup between 5 and 2000, capped at 5 s of warm-up, measure.ts:34-39, 118-138), so construction runs JIT-hot. A real cold start runs library code for the first time, interpreted or baseline-compiled, after parsing it. Tilts toward libraries whose construction is heavy but JIT-friendly; the label overstates what is measured.
Parse/evaluate of the library bundle is outside the clock (the module is loaded once per process, worker.ts:69); bundle size is measured elsewhere (src/bundle.ts) and not combined with this row.

Allocating the row objects is outside (`loadRows` built once, worker.ts:85) and the previous store is disposed untimed (`restore` calls `dropBinding`, scenarios.ts:4076-4078); where `gc` is exposed it is also collected untimed before every timed sample (measure.ts:45-47, 74; worker.ts:63-67).

Six libraries were recorded rendering an empty frame before the full one (scenarios.ts:4056-4061: mobx, legend-state, effector, nanostores, preact-signals, alien-signals, measured 2026-08-29); that cost is inside the clock for them, as it is for a user. Neutral. The record predates the 2026-10-17 upgrades of mobx (7.0.6) and nanostores (1.5.5) and was not re-checked.
card.summary: The only row with construction in the clock, but construction is warmed by repetition, so it is a hot-construction cost rather than a page-load cold start.
card.body:
## What the script does

One step: `newBinding()`, `write(loadRows)`, `settle()` (scenarios.ts:4079-4083).
`check`: at least one delivery per view and a full window A (scenarios.ts:4090-4097).
`fromEmpty` (scenarios.ts:4051) resets the consumers to forget (worker.ts:368-375),
skips the opening load (worker.ts:362) and starts the model empty.
`repeatable: false` (:4071).

## Representativeness

Opening a screen is real and per-navigation. What a user experiences at a cold
start is dominated by code that has never run; this script repeats the
construction until it is warm and reports the minimum (measure.ts:55-97). The
quantity is useful (the cost of building a store and its subscriptions in a
running application, for example on a route change that creates a per-route
store), but that is a narrower thing than "cold start to first render".
js-framework-benchmark measures startup separately (script bootup, TTI) in a real
browser.

## The standing record, checked

`ORDINARY_SCRIPT` (scenarios.ts:86-169, signed at :99). Its header says the script
"settles inside its own loop with two live consumers" (scenarios.ts:80-85); here
the two consumers exist before the clock (worker.ts:76) and the views that drive
them are built and subscribed inside it by `newBinding` (worker.ts:320-334), which
the record does not describe but does not contradict.

card.models: Disposing a whole store together with its views and every subscription — a per-route or per-widget store going away, a micro-frontend unmount, or test teardown.
card.measures: The synchronous cost of `dispose()` on a fully populated, fully subscribed binding.
favours: Libraries whose teardown is dropping references and letting the collector reclaim them: the reclamation is not timed (see biases).

Against libraries whose teardown walks every subscription and unlinks it from surviving structures (per-row effects, per-slot holds; the script's comment names `OIMEffect.detach` per per-slot effect, scenarios.ts:4105-4110).
biases: The usual navigation in an application unmounts VIEWS while a global store survives; there each unsubscribe must unlink from live structures. This script disposes the store too, so a library can skip unlinking entirely. The surviving-store case is the churn family.

GC is excluded: when the worker runs with an exposed `gc`, a forced collection runs before each timed sample (measure.ts:72-74; worker.ts:63-67), so the garbage this teardown creates is collected before the NEXT sample, outside the clock. In an application that cost lands on the main thread soon after navigation. Tilts toward drop-the-reference teardowns.

`repeatable: false` (scenarios.ts:4218) means one run per sample (the repeat cap is 1, cells/runBatch.ts:55) of a region the script's comment puts at tens of microseconds (scenarios.ts:4111-4115), so timer resolution and noise are a large share; C3's spread ceiling is likelier to refuse a rank here, as the record says (scenarios.ts:4198-4202).
The proof frame cannot tell 'refused the write' from 'accepted and stayed silent' (scenarios.ts:4253-4255); both pass.
card.summary: A real but uncommon event — the whole store disposed — whose measured cost excludes garbage collection; the everyday navigation case is an unmount against a surviving store, which this row does not ask.
card.body:
## What the script does

Restore drops the binding, builds a fresh one and loads it untimed
(scenarios.ts:4226-4231); the timed step is `dropBinding()`, which calls
`binding.dispose()` (scenarios.ts:4232-4234; worker.ts:335-339). `check` demands no
delivery during the teardown, then writes a page into the torn-down binding (a throw
is swallowed) and demands no delivery again (scenarios.ts:4241-4268). The population
audit is skipped (`populationDestroyed`, scenarios.ts:4215; worker.ts:454).

## Representativeness

Whole-store disposal happens, but for most single-page applications the store
outlives screens. The task is therefore real and infrequent. As a measurement it
captures the synchronous unlinking work only; libraries that defer everything to
the collector look free. Neither js-framework-benchmark (which measures "clear
rows", DOM-side) nor the signal benchmarks measure a store teardown, so this is a
property the suite asks that others do not, with the GC caveat above.

## The standing record, checked

Its own record (scenarios.ts:4140-4212). A1 and A3 NOT MET are stated with reasons
that match the code; standard.ts:337-345 would refuse an A1 MET here. B4 MET: the
`populationDestroyed` flag makes the step a `teardown` (floor.ts:85) and `BOUND_BY`
hands it `tearDownFloor` (floor.ts:96); see that card for what the floor is. C5 MET
holds because the controls all supply `bind` (types.ts:463; standard.ts:380-397).

card.models: Nothing an application does: a hand-built screen given back by overwriting one reference, used as the lower bound of the `tearDown` table.
card.measures: The cost of one reference store — the least any teardown can cost.
favours: No participant. As the divisor of the teardown table it makes every row's multiple a ratio against an operation of a few nanoseconds.
biases: The timed region is one assignment (scenarios.ts:3688-3690) run once per sample (`repeatable: false`, scenarios.ts:3646; repeat cap 1, cells/runBatch.ts:55). The sample is bracketed by two `process.hrtime.bigint()` calls (measure.ts:75-77), so the measured minimum is likely of the order of the timer's own overhead rather than the assignment, and the teardown multiples are then ratios to clock overhead. Not measured by this card.

The garbage released by the drop is collected before the next sample, outside the clock (measure.ts:72-74), exactly as for `tearDown`; the floor shares that exclusion, so it bounds the synchronous part only.
The screen's subscribers are closures in an array attached to nothing (scenarios.ts:3661-3673); a teardown of subscriptions to a surviving store is not what this bounds.
Windows A and B are the same rows (scenarios.ts:3659-3660), declared irrelevant to the cost (:3648-3652); true for a reference drop.
card.summary: A lower bound that is, in practice, near the timer's resolution; use it to see which teardown rows are at clock noise, not to rank them.
card.body:
## What the script does

Restore builds a `Map` of all rows, two window arrays, one closure per visible row
and two view bodies (scenarios.ts:3653-3686). The timed step sets the module
variable `floorScreen` to the shared empty screen `TORN_DOWN_SCREEN`
(scenarios.ts:3543-3550, 3688-3690). `check` runs a proof frame stronger than
`tearDown`'s: it writes a page into the torn-down screen, calls every per-row
subscriber left on it and fails if any read a label, then calls every view body and
demands nothing was delivered (scenarios.ts:3697-3724).

## Representativeness

An instrument. Its argument — a floor must be unbeatable, so clearing structures
would be a floor a reference-dropping store beats (scenarios.ts:3558-3563) — is
sound. The consequence is that the floor is essentially zero at the timer's
resolution, which makes the multiples in the teardown table large and not very
informative.

## The standing record, checked

Its own record (scenarios.ts:3583-3640). A1, A3, C5 NOT MET with reasons that match
the code (A1 is forced by standard.ts:337-345 for a `populationDestroyed` script).
B4 MET's falsifier "the teardown row coming out BELOW this number" (:3617-3619) is
unlikely to fire for the reason above, so it guards little.

card.models: An inline edit or a pushed update to one field of one row the user can see, repeated row by row, each change its own frame.
card.measures: Single-write latency from a keyed column write to a re-rendered window, plus whether an unrelated view (group B) is woken.
favours: Stores that route a row write to the views containing that row (per-row or per-visible-slot subscriptions, signal graphs) over stores that re-derive or rescan a whole group or the whole population per frame.
Nothing favours coalescing here: one write per settle and no `frame` call (scenarios.ts:465-468), so eager and deferred-flush stores do the same number of derivations.
biases: Every delivery re-formats all 32 window lines and hashes them (render.ts:31-44 `deliver`, consumer.ts:108-148), so a store that knows exactly which row changed cannot show that advantage on the render side. Real per-row-component UIs re-render one row. Tilts toward list-level derivations and compresses every gap toward the consumer constant.

`label` is neither filtered nor sorted on (dataset.ts:22-24), so a write can never change membership or order. Tilts toward stores whose window bookkeeping is expensive only on shape changes (per-visible-row subscribers: oimdb, tinybase, per WHY-EACH-ROW.md:615-629).
Rows have five short columns (dataset.ts:29-35). Copy-on-write stores (immutable entity spread) and per-field-observable stores pay less per patch than they would on application-width entities.
Only 2 of the 50 groups are watched (dataset.ts:37-41). Stores maintaining an index on all 50 groups pay maintenance nobody reads (WHY-EACH-ROW.md:559-587); tilts against eagerly indexed stores.
Timed in Node on a JIT-warm loop and reported as the minimum of samples (measure.ts:41-97). Real edits arrive sporadically into colder code; tilts toward monomorphic, JIT-friendly write paths.
card.summary: The suite's baseline single-field edit: real and frequent, but the full-window string render per delivery makes much of every row the consumer's cost rather than the store's.

## What the script does

`WINDOW` steps (32 at the default point, dataset.ts:63; N = 10 000, registry.ts:170
and cells/points.ts:4). Each step is `patchLabel(id, label)` on the next row of view
A's window, then `settle()` (scenarios.ts:460-469). The two label sets alternate with
a suffix so a repeat inside one sample never writes a value already stored
(scenarios.ts:457-466). `check` demands exactly 32 distinct renders of A and 0 of B
(scenarios.ts:470-472); the oracle replays the same writes against the plain-Map
model with one `emit` per write (scenarios.ts:473-482, oracle.ts:400-403).

## Representativeness

A one-field edit to a visible row is among the most common things a list or table
screen does: inline editing, an optimistic update, a socket message for one row.
32 consecutive single-row frames is a reasonable stand-in for a burst of such
messages. The size (10 000 rows, 50 groups of 200, 32 visible) matches a mid-sized
table screen.

This is the closest analogue in the suite to js-framework-benchmark's "partial
update" — but that benchmark updates every 10th row in ONE frame, which here is
`batchPatch`. js-framework-benchmark also measures the DOM; this suite's consumer
is a string formatter, so render cost is uniform across libraries and keyed-row
reconciliation is not modelled at all.

## The standing record, checked

`ORDINARY_SCRIPT` (scenarios.ts:86-169, signed for this key at :88). For this script
its claims hold as far as the code shows: A1 (:106-110) — every step produces a
distinct render of A (check at scenarios.ts:471); B4 (:140-144) — the step is a
window delivery: `stepDeliveryOf` returns `window` (floor.ts:86) and `floorKeyFor`
maps it to `consumerFloor` (floor.ts:95, 144-147). Whether that floor is a true
bound is the `consumerFloor` card's question.

## What it does not cover

A write to a column a view filters or sorts on (`moveGroup`, `sortKeyMove` cover
those separately); a write to a row whose entity is wide; a write arriving while
the consumer is mid-render or under a scheduler (React batching, microtasks) —
`settle` is synchronous and nothing in the suite yields.

card.models: An update to a row that belongs to the list on screen but is scrolled out of view (virtualised list, paginated table), one row per frame.
card.measures: Wake-up selectivity at sub-group granularity: whether a write to a watched-but-invisible row wakes the view, and what that wake costs.
favours: Stores whose views subscribe to the VISIBLE rows (per-visible-slot subscriptions; the script's own comment says the design that benefited from every write landing inside the window is 'ours', scenarios.ts:485-491) — they hear nothing.
Fine-grained computeds that track only the properties of the rows they returned (MobX-style), for the same reason.
Against: stores whose view is a derivation over the whole group or the whole population; each write wakes it, it re-derives an unchanged window and delivers redundantly.
biases: `label` is not a filter or sort column and the rows are the second window of group A (`outsideA`, dataset.ts:1030; documented at :478-484), so a write can never pull a row into view. The case where an off-screen row's SORT KEY moves it on screen — what makes visible-row-only subscription hard — is not asked here.

Redundant deliveries are timed with their full 32-line render (render.ts:31-44), so a waking store pays the consumer for nothing. That matches an application that re-renders on a wake, and makes the row's gaps partly consumer cost.

ADDRESSED: the window floor. The script sets `rendersNothing` (scenarios.ts:501), so `stepDeliveryOf` returns `nothing` (floor.ts:79), `floorKeyFor` returns no floor (floor.ts:91-100, 144-147), and the table prints `no floor` (floor.ts:191) with the reason from `UNBOUNDED_BECAUSE` (floor.ts:129-136).
With no floor, a row that wakes keeps its consumer share; the wake count is the subject, so that is the intended reading.
card.summary: A real and frequent case — edits to off-screen rows of a virtualised list — that prices subscription scope; it carries no floor multiple, which fits a script whose correct answer delivers nothing.
card.body:
## What the script does

32 steps; each patches `label` on one row of `plan.outsideA`, view A's own group
ranked immediately below its window, and settles (scenarios.ts:515-524). Neither
view may produce a distinct render (scenarios.ts:525-527). Restore writes the
original labels back untimed (scenarios.ts:506-513). A dropped write is caught by
the population audit (worker.ts:462; oracle.ts:526-528 compares `label`).

## Representativeness

Virtualised lists and paged tables hold far more rows than they show; writes to the
hidden part are at least as frequent as writes to the visible part. This is the
right question to ask and few public benchmarks ask it: js-framework-benchmark
renders every row, and signal benchmarks have no notion of a window.

## The standing record, checked

`SILENT_SCRIPT` (scenarios.ts:171-187, signed for this key at :172).

- A1 NOT MET (:175-180), with the reason that a correct store renders nothing.
- B4 MET (:181-186): the falsifier is a window floor scaling this table, which does
  not happen. The load check accepts it through the declared `nothing` shape
  (standard.ts:451-460). The item's demand — the consumer's cost measured and kept
  out (standard.ts:156) — is not met in substance, and `UNBOUNDED_BECAUSE` says so
  (floor.ts:133-135); the MET records that no wrong floor is applied.
- The rest is `ORDINARY_SCRIPT` (spread at :174) and holds for this script.

## What it does not cover

An off-screen row whose own RANK write should bring it on screen: no script writes
the rank of a row outside the window. Off-screen rows do enter view A when visible
rows are deleted (`outsideA` is what the deletion scenario refills from,
dataset.ts:60-61), and a row from another group enters view B's window on
`moveGroup` and `moveAndReorder` (dataset.ts:629-638); neither is a sort-key move
from outside the window.

card.models: An update to a field of a visible row that this screen does not display (a timestamp, a sync flag, a hidden attribute), one row per frame.
card.measures: Column granularity of change tracking: whether 'the entity changed' is distinguished from 'something the view reads changed'.
favours: Stores that track dependencies per property (MobX observables, per-field signals): the column has no observers, so nothing runs.
Against: row-granular stores — a whole-row signal, a per-visible-row subscription, an immutable row replaced on write — which wake view A once per step to show identical text.
biases: `note` is read by NOTHING anywhere (dataset.ts:25-27), an extreme. In applications an unread-here column is usually read by some other view; the script prices only the best case for per-property tracking.

The drop-the-write cheat is not caught by the digest (scenarios.ts:544-556 says so); it is caught only by the population audit after the run, which compares `note` on every row (worker.ts:462; oracle.ts:529-531). A failure there voids the row, so the bias is closed, but only by the audit.
Narrow rows (dataset.ts:29-35): a per-field-signal store pays its per-field setup at load, which is not timed here, so this row shows its benefit and hides its cost.

ADDRESSED: the window floor. `rendersNothing` is set (scenarios.ts:567), so `stepDeliveryOf` returns `nothing` (floor.ts:79), `floorKeyFor` finds no floor for it (floor.ts:91-100, 144-147), and the table prints `no floor` (floor.ts:191) with the reason from `UNBOUNDED_BECAUSE` (floor.ts:129-136).
card.summary: The isolation half of the patchColumn pair: it prices per-property versus per-row change tracking on a column nobody reads, and is meaningful only beside patchColumn and batchPatchNote.

## What the script does

The same 32 rows, count and step shape as `patchColumn`, writing `note` instead of
`label` (scenarios.ts:580-589). Both views must produce zero distinct renders
(scenarios.ts:590-592); the oracle emits per write and produces the unchanged
state because the model renders `id rank label` (scenarios.ts:593-604).

## Representativeness

Real, but one corner: in an application the visible row typically carries fields
that this view does not render, and server pushes often touch only those. How
often a field is truly read by no one is application-specific. As a measurement
of a single design axis it is clean, because it differs from `patchColumn` only in
the column (scenarios.ts:539-542, description :562-565). Read as a workload alone,
it overweights the case where per-property tracking wins outright.

## The standing record, checked

`SILENT_SCRIPT` (scenarios.ts:171-187, signed for this key at :172). A1 NOT MET with
its reason (:175-180). B4 MET (:181-186) records that no window floor is applied;
`standard.ts:451-460` accepts the absence because `nothing` has an
`UNBOUNDED_BECAUSE` entry. The consumer share of a waking row is not removed, by
design (floor.ts:133-135). The same holds on `patchOutsideWindow`.

card.models: A sync response or bulk edit: about a tenth of the population changes one visible field, applied in one frame.
card.measures: Cost of many writes before one frame boundary — whether the store coalesces deliveries, and how much of a widely spread batch reaches the two watched views.
favours: Stores whose delivery is deferred to `settle` (a dirty flag, a frame-scoped delivery list): one derivation and one render per view whatever the library's batching API.

Libraries with a batching API, which `ctx.binding.frame` reaches (scenarios.ts:656-660; `TBinding.frame`, types.ts:24-26): `runInAction`, `batch` or `transaction` around the 1000 writes defers their reactions to the end of the scope, so they also derive once per view.
Against libraries with no batching API: their `frame` is a plain call and they deliver once per visible write.
biases: One `patchLabel` per row (scenarios.ts:656-660). A library whose bulk idiom is ONE action carrying many updates cannot use it: merging the calls would be the adapter holding values the library does not hold, which B3 forbids (scenarios.ts:135-139). Redux Toolkit's adapter defers listener notification to the end of the frame with autoBatch (adapters/redux-toolkit.ts:72-101, actions prepared with `prepareAutoBatched` at :193-261), so its listeners run once; what the row still charges it for is 1000 reducer passes where an application would dispatch one action.

A library with no batch API delivers per visible write, and every delivery re-derives and renders the full window synchronously (render.ts:31-43). An application under a UI scheduler would coalesce those renders; the consumer here has none.

The stride is stepped down to be coprime with the 50 groups so every group is reached (dataset.ts:813-814), and both windows are forced to be hit (dataset.ts:817-848). A handful of the ~1000 writes are visible. Realistic for a sync response.
`finalStateOnly` (scenarios.ts:636): the render count is reported, not judged, so the time column mixes one-render and many-render rows under one label. The counters column says which is which.
card.summary: A bulk response in one frame, run inside each library's own batch scope; what remains tilted is the per-row call shape, which action-based stores cannot fold into one action.
