## What the script does

One step. Inside `ctx.binding.frame`, `patchLabel` on every id of `plan.batch` —
`max(4·WINDOW, N/10)` rows, 1000 at the default point (`BATCH_FRACTION`,
dataset.ts:690, 799-802; `DEFAULT_N`, registry.ts:170) — then ONE `settle()`
(scenarios.ts:651-662). Labels alternate between two suffixes per run so a repeat
is a change (:653-654). `check` asks that both windows are full and A's rows are
still in window order (scenarios.ts:673-689); the text is judged by the
final-state comparison (`adapterAnswer`/`oracleAnswer`, worker.ts:419-450; final
state sent from the verify pass, worker.ts:504-514) and every write by the
population audit (worker.ts:462).

## Ways a broken store passes

- **Intermediate states are not judged.** With `finalStateOnly` only the ending
  state of each view is compared. A store that delivered a wrong intermediate
  window and then the right final one passes; for a one-step script with
  correct libraries delivering 1 to ~5 states per view that is the intended
  trade.
- **View B's order is not checked by `check`**, only its row count (:687); its
  text is compared by the final-state digest.

## Why the verdict is representative

The workload is js-framework-benchmark's "partial update" shape at store level,
and with `frame` an eager library can apply its documented batch across the
frame. The description states the outcome per class of library
(scenarios.ts:625-630): once per view for a deferred store or an honoured batch
scope, once per visible row for a library with no batch API.

## The standing record, checked

`ORDINARY_SCRIPT` (scenarios.ts:86-169, listed at :89). B3 holds: no adapter is
allowed to hold values the library does not hold, and `frame` gives a library its
own scope without the adapter doing the library's job. B1 holds for libraries
with a batch scope; for libraries without one, the many-delivery asymmetry is
printed only in the counters. B4: one step, `stepDeliveryOf` returns `window`
(floor.ts:86) and `BOUND_BY` scales it by `consumerFloor` (floor.ts:95); a
correct store delivers both views, so the floor understates the minimum — safe
direction.

card.models: A bulk sync that changes only fields this screen does not display, applied in one frame.
card.measures: Whether coalescing at the frame boundary recovers the wasted wake-ups a row-granular store pays on an unread column, versus per-property tracking that never wakes.
favours: Per-property trackers (mobx-style): nothing observes `note`, so no reaction runs at all, batched or not.
Row-granular stores that defer delivery to `settle`, and row-granular libraries whose batch API `frame` reaches (scenarios.ts:752-756): at most one redundant derivation per view per frame.
Against row-granular libraries with no batching API: one redundant derivation and one full-window render per visible write in the batch.
biases: The script sets `rendersNothing` (scenarios.ts:733), so `stepDeliveryOf` returns `nothing` (floor.ts:79) and no floor divides the table (`BOUND_BY` has no `nothing` entry, floor.ts:91-100); the reason is printed from `UNBOUNDED_BECAUSE` (floor.ts:129-136).

With no floor, the consumer's share of a row that does wake is not taken out of it (floor.ts:131-135 says so). Wakes are the subject here, so that is the intended reading, but B4's demand is not met in substance (see standing).
`note` is read by nothing (dataset.ts:25-27), an extreme that makes per-property tracking free; it says little about a column read by some views and not others.

One `patchNote` call per row (scenarios.ts:752-756): an action-based store cannot fold them into one action, as on `batchPatch`. Redux Toolkit's listener calls are deferred to the frame end by autoBatch (adapters/redux-toolkit.ts:72-101); its 1000 reducer passes are not.
card.summary: An isolation instrument bracketing patchNote and batchPatch; it prices coalescing against column routing, with each library's own batch scope and no false floor.
card.body:
## What the script does

The same stride and count as `batchPatch` (`plan.batch`, 1000 rows at the default
point), writing `note` inside `ctx.binding.frame`, with one `settle()` after it
(scenarios.ts:747-758). Both views must produce zero distinct renders
(scenarios.ts:759-761). The oracle writes the notes and emits once; the model
renders `id rank label`, so its state is the one before (:762-773). The writes
are proved only by the population audit (worker.ts:462).

## Ways a broken store passes

- **A store that dropped every `note` write** passes `check` and the digest; it
  fails only the population audit, which compares every column of every row
  (`firstPopulationMismatch`, oracle.ts:507, run at worker.ts:462). That audit runs in
  both passes (`auditStore`, worker.ts:498, 660), so the hole is closed there and
  nowhere else.

## Representativeness

A sync that only touches undisplayed fields does happen (bookkeeping columns,
server timestamps), but the script is built as the fourth corner of a 2×2 —
{one write, batch} × {read column, unread column} — and its own comment says so
(scenarios.ts:704-719). As a workload on its own it would overweight the case
where per-property tracking is free. Read it only against `patchNote` and
`batchPatch`. The description says the per-write delivery applies to a library
with no batch API (scenarios.ts:727-729).

## The standing record, checked

`SILENT_SCRIPT` (scenarios.ts:171-187, listed at :172): `ORDINARY_SCRIPT` with A1
and B4 replaced.

- A1 NOT MET (:175-180), with the reason that a correct store renders nothing.
- B4 MET (:181-185), falsifier: a window floor scaling this table. The load check
  accepts it because the `nothing` shape's absence of a floor is declared
  (standard.ts:443-460). The item's demand is that the consumer's own cost be
  measured and kept out of the reading (standard.ts:156); here it is neither, by
  design. The MET records that no wrong floor is applied, not that the demand is
  met.

card.models: A dense update: half of every group changes a visible field in each of two consecutive frames (a full refresh, a price tick across a whole book, a recompute of every row's status).
card.measures: Cost of a frame where the dirty set is a large fraction of the subscribed population, and what that frame leaves behind for the next.
favours: Designs that scan subscribers or rebuild at the boundary rather than maintain a per-write dirty list; the script's comment predicts the engine's rejected stamp-and-scan arm ahead by about 1.18x at this fraction (scenarios.ts:780-785; dataset.ts:101-106) — an internal figure, not verified here.
Deferred-flush stores and libraries whose batch API `frame` opens (scenarios.ts:844-848), over adapters whose `frame` is a direct call.
biases: Each frame's 5000 writes run inside `ctx.binding.frame` (scenarios.ts:844-848; types.ts:24-26). Every adapter now supplies `frame`: a batch scope where it declares one (mobx `runInAction`, mobx.ts:40-42; legend-state `batch`, legend-state.ts:69-71; oimdb `openSubframe`/`closeSubframe`; tinybase transaction; signaldb `collection.batch`), and a direct `run()` in the anchors, lokijs (lokijs.ts:96), oimdb-legacy, nanostores (nanostores.ts:39-41) and effector (effector.ts:39-41). Whether each direct call is a library with no batch API or an adapter that skipped one is the participant cards' question.
5000 separate `patchLabel` calls per frame (scenarios.ts:845-847). Refresh-style frames usually arrive as one array; an action-based store cannot fold the calls into one action, as on `batchPatch`.
Only two frames (DIRTY_FRAMES, dataset.ts:95). 'The frame after a large frame' is asked once; a steady state of dense frames is not.

A contiguous prefix of the population (dataset.ts:850-856; `TPlan.dirty`, :516-522) dealt round-robin: every group is half dirty. Real dense updates are clustered (one table, one feed); here every group's derivation is invalidated.
The labels are built with a template literal inside the timed loop (scenarios.ts:846): the allocation is paid alike by every row.

ADDRESSED: `check` now asks for at least DIRTY_FRAMES DISTINCT renders per view (scenarios.ts:871-872), not deliveries, so a store that re-delivered an unchanged window in frame 1 fails it. The comment above it still says 'delivered at least once per frame' (:852-859); the code asks the stronger thing.
card.summary: The dense end of the write dial, which the rest of the suite never reaches; real for refresh-style frames and run inside each adapter's `frame`, but two round-robin frames of per-row calls are one corner of that behaviour.
card.body:
## What the script does

`DIRTY_FRAMES` = 2 steps (dataset.ts:95; scenarios.ts:812). Each writes `label` on
every row of `plan.dirty` — the first N/2 rows, 5000 at the default point
(dataset.ts:852-854) — inside `ctx.binding.frame`, with a per-frame mark from
`DIRTY_MARKS` so no write is a no-op (scenarios.ts:432-434, 839-851), then one
`settle()`. `check`: view A full and in window order, view B full, and at least two
distinct renders per view (scenarios.ts:860-874). The final state is compared with
the model (`finalStateOnly`, :816; worker.ts:504-513).

## Representativeness

Whole-table refreshes exist (polling a dashboard, a market data tick, a
recalculation) and are exactly where per-write bookkeeping costs most; no other
script here goes above about 10% dirty (`batchPatch`'s BATCH_FRACTION, dataset.ts:690).
That makes the row necessary. It is narrow because the shape is fixed — exactly half
of every group, two frames — and because the frame is 5000 separate calls rather than
one array write.

## The standing record, checked

`ORDINARY_SCRIPT` (scenarios.ts:86-169, signed for this key at :90). B1 (:125-129):
the eager-versus-deferred asymmetry now shows only for adapters whose `frame` is a
direct call. B4 (:140-144): both views change per frame and the floor counts one
window delivery per step (floor.ts:86, 95) — the safe direction, since an eager
store delivers more than one.

card.models: One socket or sync frame that carries every kind of change at once: rows created, rows deleted, a visible field edited, rows moved to another list, and rows re-ranked inside the visible list.
card.measures: The cost of applying five different write kinds inside one frame and producing the final window of both views once, including whatever ordered structure the store keeps for the group.
favours: Stores that defer derivation to the frame boundary, or libraries whose batching API is honoured by `frame` (scenarios.ts:933-943): they derive each view once over the finished frame.

Designs that re-derive one window from scratch, because every one of the 19 row changes lands in view A's window or at the head of view B's, so incremental maintenance has no off-screen work to skip. Direction asserted from the shape of the sets, not measured.
Against libraries with no batching API at all: their `frame` is a plain call, so each of the 13 binding calls can deliver on its own.
biases: All five sets sit inside view A's window by construction (dataset.ts:940-965, 1092-1096): movers in slots 0-3, patched rows in slots 4-6 at the default window, sorters at slots 7, 9, 11, 13 (dataset.ts:779-793), the deleted set in slots 28-31. A real frame from a server touches mostly rows nobody is looking at; `batchPatch` asks that half.

Movers arrive in group B at their resting ranks 1-4, which are below every other row (dataset.ts:440-447, 630-637), so each arrival is at position 0 of view B, the cheapest insertion into an ordered bucket. `moveAndReorder` is the script meant to ask the mid-order arrival.

Small: 4 inserts, 4 deletes, 3 label patches, 4 group moves and 4 rank moves at the default point (MOVER_COUNT and SORTER_COUNT, dataset.ts:69-71; sorter count dataset.ts:779-782; patched slice dataset.ts:955). The row is dominated by per-frame overhead and two window derivations, not by write volume.

The inserted rows are cloned once in `prepare` (scenarios.ts:910-918) and the same objects are written in every sample, after the untimed restore removed them (scenarios.ts:919-930). A store that keeps the objects it is given sees the same identities each time; whether any participant has an identity-keyed cache this helps is not verified.
`finalStateOnly` (scenarios.ts:908): torn intermediate states produced by a library without a batch API cost time but are not judged. Sound for a frame whose render count is the store's answer.
card.summary: A realistic mixed frame, small and concentrated on the visible window, whose correctness is pinned by the final-state comparison and the population audit rather than by `check` alone.
card.body:
## What the script does

One step, one `settle` (scenarios.ts:931-945). Inside `ctx.binding.frame` it calls
`write` with the inserted rows, `remove` with the tail of view A's window, three
`patchLabel`, four `setGroup` to group B and four `setRank` to each sorter's `low`
rank. The five sets are disjoint and `makePlan` throws if the window is too small
to keep them so (dataset.ts:944-954).

## What decides correctness

`check` (scenarios.ts:946-954) asks for two full windows, view A's head to be an
inserted row (only those ids start with `m`: dataset.ts:959 against `r`, `f`, `h`
at dataset.ts:437, 910, 930), and at least one delivery per view. That alone is
weak: a store that applied only the insert would pass it. The strength is
elsewhere: `finalStateOnly` makes the verify and the timed processes compare the
digest and row count of the state both views are left showing against the model
(worker.ts:419-447, 501-512, 647-661), and the population and grouping audits read
the stored rows and all fifty buckets afterwards (worker.ts:462-464). The final
state differs from the starting one in every set, so a store that dropped any of
the five writes fails one of those. No case found where a broken store passes.

## Representativeness

A subscription push or sync response that mixes creates, deletes, edits and moves
is common in collaborative and real-time applications, and no other script here
issues more than one write kind per frame. The size is small and the placement is
the most visible possible, so read it as "one busy visible frame" and read
`batchPatch` for the wide, mostly invisible one.

## The standing record, checked

`ORDINARY_SCRIPT` (scenarios.ts:86-169, signed at :101). A1 holds: the head check
forces a changed state. B4: the table is scaled by `consumerFloor` (one window
delivery per step, floor.ts:76-87, 95); a correct step changes both views, so the
minimum consumer work is two deliveries and the floor understates it; the
multiple errs high, which is the safe direction. C5 holds only if every control
arm implements `frame`; `control.ts` does at the time of reading (control.ts:228,
546, 801, 1045, 1138).

card.models: A card moved between two columns of a board, or a row whose status changes so it leaves one filtered list and joins another, one move per frame.
card.measures: Re-selection: removing a row from one grouped view and inserting it into another, with both windows re-rendered every step.
favours: Stores keeping an ordered bucket per group: every arrival is at POSITION 0 of the target order, the cheapest insertion such a bucket has; `TPlan.arrivalRanks` says so and that it was chosen to make the move visible rather than to be typical (dataset.ts:629-638).
Stores with a group index over those that rescan the population per derivation.
biases: Movers are the first MOVER_COUNT rows of group A by ordinal and are ranked 1..4, below every other row (dataset.ts:440-448), so they sit at the head of whichever group they are in. Arrival is always at position 0 and departure always from the head. Tilts toward ordered-bucket designs (oimdb among them) whose insertion cost grows with position; `moveAndReorder` (scenarios.ts:1012-1066) exists to counter this and must be read beside it.
One write per settle (scenarios.ts:987-995) and no `frame` call: coalescing is not exercised, which is neutral between eager and deferred stores.
Only four movers and eight steps (dataset.ts:69; scenarios.ts:977): a small sample of the operation, folded by `repeat` for resolution.

Both views change every step, so the selective-wake question is not asked here; a board with 50 columns would ask which other 48 are woken (that is `consumerPerGroup`, on rank moves rather than group moves).
card.summary: A real board or status-change operation, measured at its cheapest arrival position; read it only beside moveAndReorder.
card.body:
## What the script does

`MOVER_COUNT × 2` = 8 steps (scenarios.ts:977). The first four move each mover from
group A to group B, the last four move them back, each followed by `settle()`
(scenarios.ts:987-995). `check` demands exactly eight distinct renders in each view
(scenarios.ts:996-998); the oracle replays the same moves with one `emit` per move
(scenarios.ts:999-1007). `restore` puts every mover back in group A (scenarios.ts:983-986).

## Representativeness

Changing a row's group is the core operation of a kanban board and of any
status-filtered list, so the task is typical. The size — one row per frame — is
typical of a drag. What is not typical is that the moved row always lands at the
head of the target list; in a board the card lands where the user drops it, and in
a status list it lands at its sort position. The plan's own comment admits the
choice (dataset.ts:629-638), and `moveAndReorder` asks the mid-order arrival with
`plan.arrivalRanks` (dataset.ts:967-990).

## The standing record, checked

`ORDINARY_SCRIPT` (scenarios.ts:86-169, signed for this key at :91). A1 MET
(:106-110) holds: both views render a new state every step. B4 MET (:140-144) holds:
`stepDeliveryOf` returns `window` (floor.ts:86) and `BOUND_BY` maps it to
`consumerFloor` (floor.ts:95).

card.models: A row changes list and position together: a task dragged into another column at a chosen place, a ticket re-assigned with a new priority.
card.measures: The cost of a group move combined with a rank change in one frame, where the arrival is in the middle of the target window rather than at its head: one run per sample, each after an untimed restore.
favours: Stores whose ordered bucket inserts by search over stores that append and re-sort; the arrival point is mid-window, so a head-only fast path does not help. Direction not measured.

Libraries whose batching API `frame` reaches: the two writes of a step become one state. Libraries with no batching API render the intermediate state (group changed, rank not yet) and pay an extra derivation per step.
biases: Four movers, four steps (MOVER_COUNT, dataset.ts:69). Arrival ranks are adjacent integers in one gap of view B (dataset.ts:967-990, `inB[arrivalSlot].rank + 1 + j`), so every mover arrives at nearly the same slot.
The way back to group A is the untimed restore (scenarios.ts:1033-1040), so the timed half is only the mid-window arrival; the head-of-group departure it pairs with is `moveGroup`'s cost too.
card.summary: The mid-order arrival is real, its end state is verified, and every timed run is a real move (`repeatable: false`, one run per sample after restore); narrow because four arrivals land in one gap of one window.
card.body:
## What the script does

`MOVER_COUNT` = 4 steps (scenarios.ts:1026). Each step calls `setGroup(mover, B)` and
`setRank(mover, arrivalRank)` inside `ctx.binding.frame` and settles (:1041-1051); the
oracle replays the same two writes with one `emit` per step (:1057-1065). `restore` puts
every mover back in group A at the rank captured in `prepare` (:1030-1040) before each
sample.

## What `check` and the final state prove

`finalStateOnly` (:1028) makes the final state the judge, and the final state is the
one the moves produced: every mover sits in group B at its arrival rank. A store that
lost a `setRank` places that mover at its resting rank (1 to 4, below every other row of
B; dataset.ts:440-447), so view B ends with a different line order than the model's and
the verify pass fails it. `check` (:1052-1056) additionally asks at least `MOVER_COUNT`
distinct states in each view over the run (a total, not one per step) and both windows
full.

## Why the verdict is narrow

`repeatable: false` (scenarios.ts:1029) caps `repeat` at 1 (cells/runBatch.ts:55), so
each sample is one run after `restore`, and every timed `setGroup`/`setRank` writes a
value the store does not already hold. What keeps it at `narrow`: four arrivals into one
gap of one window is one corner of drag-and-drop, read beside `moveGroup` (arrival at the
head) and `sortKeyMove` (a move inside one window).

## The standing record, checked

`ORDINARY_SCRIPT` (scenarios.ts:86-169, signed at :102). C2 MET's falsifier concerns the
sampling plan's source; with one run per sample there is no rerun for it to miss. B4: one window delivery per step (floor.ts:76-87, 95), while a
correct step changes both views, so the floor understates the minimum.

## History of this card

An earlier version rated the script `misleading` because the run ended with every mover
back in group A, so a store that dropped the rank write passed. The script was changed to
end in group B and return through `restore`, which closed that; the previous card rated it
`narrow`. A later version rated it `misleading` again because that same change left
`repeatable: true` in place, so up to 511 of every sample's runs rewrote values already
held. The script now says `repeatable: false`, and the verify pass's repeatability guard
(worker.ts, `secondRunFailure`) fails any script that claims to be repeatable and is not.

card.models: A row's sort key changes so it moves within the visible list — a priority change, a re-ranked item, a drag within one column — one move per frame.
card.measures: Order maintenance for a single moved row inside a window whose membership does not change.
favours: Stores with an incrementally maintained ordered index (insertion repair of one row) over stores that re-sort the group or rescan the population per derivation.
Against stores that subscribe per visible row and re-point subscriptions whenever the window's shape changes (oimdb and tinybase per WHY-EACH-ROW.md:615-629): an order change is a shape change.
biases: View A's sorters are the rows at slots lowAnchor+2, +4, +6, +8 of the window (slots 7, 9, 11, 13 at WINDOW 32), and their targets are one rank past the anchors at slots lowAnchor and highAnchor (5 and 25), plus j (dataset.ts:779-793). Both targets are inside the window and the mover is never an anchor, so membership never changes. This isolates reordering cleanly and excludes the common case where a rank change moves a row into or out of the window.

Unlike the per-group sorters (`sorterInWindow`, dataset.ts:692-742), view A's anchors are not searched for a strict rank increase; a rank tie at an anchor could make a step render the order it already had. That would fail `check` for every adapter alike rather than tilt the row; it does not occur at the shipped points as far as this card can tell, which is unverified.
Four sorters, eight steps (dataset.ts:71; scenarios.ts:1077): small and folded by `repeat`.
View B must not change (scenarios.ts:1097): selectivity against an unrelated group is asked; selectivity inside group A (rows outside the window) is not.
card.summary: The single-row reorder every sorted list performs; its window-internal moves exclude the membership change a real sort-key update often causes.
card.body:
## What the script does

`SORTER_COUNT × 2` = 8 steps; each moves one sorter's `rank` to its low then its
high target, both strictly inside view A's window, and settles (scenarios.ts:1086-1094).
A must produce 8 distinct renders, B none (scenarios.ts:1095-1097). `restore` writes
each sorter's resting rank back (:1082-1085).

## Representativeness

A sorted list reacting to a changed key is ordinary application work (leaderboard
entries, priority edits, last-activity sort). One change per frame is the typical
rate. The anchors are fractions of the window (dataset.ts:779-780), so the distance
moved scales with `BENCH_WINDOW` and the runner's `wide` point (window 100,
cells/points.ts:5) exercises a longer move.

The analogue in js-framework-benchmark is "swap rows" (two rows exchange
positions); that benchmark's cost is in the DOM move, which this suite does not
model.

## The standing record, checked

`ORDINARY_SCRIPT` (scenarios.ts:86-169, signed for this key at :92). The claims hold
for this script: A1 — every step changes A's order; B4 — a window delivery scaled by
`consumerFloor` (floor.ts:86, 95).

card.models: Every visible row's sort key changes in the same frame — a live leaderboard or price list re-ordering on each tick — for eight ticks.
card.measures: Order maintenance as a function of how much of the order moved: a whole window re-ordered per frame, against `sortKeyMove`'s one row.
favours: Stores that sort lazily at derivation time (sort the window's candidates once per frame) over stores that maintain an ordered index incrementally — the script's comment expects the incremental bucket to lose here (scenarios.ts:1113-1125).

Deferred-flush stores and libraries whose batch API `frame` opens (scenarios.ts:1180-1184): 32 rank writes become one derivation. Adapters whose `frame` is a direct call re-derive per write if the library is eager.
biases: The 32 writes of each frame run inside `ctx.binding.frame` (scenarios.ts:1180-1184; types.ts:24-26). Every adapter supplies `frame`; it is a direct `run()` in the anchors, lokijs, oimdb-legacy, nanostores and effector (see the patchMostRows card for the lines). Whether each is a library with no batch API is the participant cards' question.

Membership is constructed never to change: the rank pool is strictly below every rank outside the window (`TPlan.resortRanks`, dataset.ts:525-534; built at :1019-1026, 1066; scenarios.ts:1127-1131). A real tick re-orders rows into and out of the window as well; this asks only the permutation.

The pool is rotated by frame+1 places (scenarios.ts:1174-1187): a structured permutation, not a random one. An insertion-based repair sees the same displacement pattern every frame. Direction unverified.

The comment's mechanism names `settleBudget(n)` in `engine/bucket/array/OIMBucketSlotsServiceArrayDriven.ts` (scenarios.ts:1115-1120); no symbol of that name exists under packages/core/src. The mechanism exists under another name: the default `bucketFullSortGuard` is `fullSortGuardAboveLogBudget` (packages/core/src/engine/bucket/array/OIMBucketSlotsServiceArrayDriven.ts:37; utils/fullSortGuardAboveLogBudget.ts:1-7), which chooses `list.sort` when `2 * outOfPlace + arrived` exceeds twice the bit length of the bucket size (16 for a 200-row bucket), else insertion repair (OIMBucketSlotsServiceArrayDriven.ts:249-263). A whole window out of place is far above that budget, so the comment's prediction follows from current code; its symbol name is stale.
32 separate `setRank` calls per frame (scenarios.ts:1181-1183): a tick usually arrives as one array, and an action-based store cannot fold the calls into one action, as on `batchPatch`.
ADDRESSED: `check` now asks for at least RESORT_FRAMES DISTINCT renders of view A (scenarios.ts:1204), not deliveries, so a store delivering an unchanged order on an intermediate frame fails it.
card.summary: The many-rows-reorder end of the sort dial, real for ticking ranked lists and run inside each adapter's `frame`, but with membership frozen and a structured permutation.
card.body:
## What the script does

`RESORT_FRAMES` = 8 steps (dataset.ts:117; scenarios.ts:1146). Each writes `rank` on
all 32 rows of view A's window from a fixed pool rotated one place further each
frame, inside `ctx.binding.frame`, then one `settle()` (scenarios.ts:1174-1187).
`check`: A full, B no distinct render, and at least 8 distinct renders of A
(scenarios.ts:1197-1204). The order itself is judged by the final-state comparison
(`finalStateOnly`, :1151; worker.ts:504-513).

## Representativeness

Whole-window re-ordering happens in live dashboards and ranked feeds; it is the
counterweight to `sortKeyMove`, which only asks an ordered index for the case it
is best at. The operation is real. It is narrow because membership cannot move and
because a tick of that kind usually arrives as a single array write, while the
script issues 32 separate `setRank` calls.

A user-initiated sort change — clicking a column header so the COMPARATOR changes —
is a different task, and the suite has no script for it.

## The standing record, checked

`ORDINARY_SCRIPT` (scenarios.ts:86-169, signed for this key at :93). B1's
eager-versus-deferred asymmetry (:125-129) now shows only for adapters whose `frame`
is a direct call.

card.models: A screen with one live view per group (fifty board columns or fifty dashboard widgets) where one group's order changes per frame.
card.measures: Wake-up selectivity across many standing views: how many of the 49 unaffected consumers are woken per write.
favours: Stores with a per-group change signal (a bucket or index per group with its own subscribers): 50 deliveries for 50 steps.
Against a single global change signal: 50 × 50 deliveries, each a full 32-line render (scenarios.ts:1241-1249).
Stores that maintain all 50 group indexes are no longer charged for unread groups here (WHY-EACH-ROW.md:559-587).
biases: The consumer is 50 times larger for a non-selective store: each redundant wake formats and hashes 32 lines (render.ts `deliver`; consumer.ts:108-147). The gap is mostly consumer cost multiplied by wake count, which WHY-EACH-ROW.md:589-600 states; the ratio is not a store-only ratio.

Fifty standing windows of 32 rows is 1600 rendered rows, larger than a typical screen. Real many-view screens (boards, dashboards) usually show fewer rows per view; the size inflates the non-selective penalty.

Each step is a rank move inside one window (scenarios.ts:1266-1276), a shape change; stores that re-point per-visible-row subscriptions on shape change (oimdb, tinybase) pay it 50 times per run, linear in the window (WHY-EACH-ROW.md:615-629). Tilts against them at the wide point, toward them at the default.
Bind-time cost of fifty views is outside the clock (`rebuild: false`, scenarios.ts:1253; WHY-EACH-ROW.md:610-614).
card.summary: The only many-views selectivity probe in the suite; real in kind (boards, dashboards) but oversized per view, so its gaps are dominated by consumer re-renders.
card.body:
## What the script does

`GROUPS` = 50 steps over `bindPerGroup` (`steps`, `perGroup: true`,
scenarios.ts:1251-1252). Step i moves group i's sorter between its `low` and
`high` ranks, both inside group i's own window, and settles
(scenarios.ts:1266-1276); `restore` puts every sorter back at `rest` and resets
`fanTurn` (:1258-1265). Every one of the fifty consumers must produce exactly one
distinct render and keep a full window (scenarios.ts:1284-1294). The oracle emits
to all fifty every step (`emitEveryGroup`, scenarios.ts:1295-1303), so it judges
content, never who woke. The worker folds the fifty digests and sums their
counters (worker.ts:419-434).

## Representativeness

Selectivity over many views is a real property and an important one; the
two-view wiring cannot ask it (WHY-EACH-ROW.md:546-557). The workload shape is a
board with all columns visible. It is narrow because the operation is fixed to a
rank move (a group move would touch two consumers, which is the board's common
case), and because 50 full windows overstate the render cost of a wake.

## The standing record, checked

`ORDINARY_SCRIPT` (scenarios.ts:86-169, signed at :94). B4 MET: the table is
scaled by `consumerFloor`, one window delivery per step (`perGroup` is not a
wiring flag `stepDeliveryOf` reads, so it falls to `window`, floor.ts:76-87,
95). For a selective store that is a bound; a non-selective store pays up to 50
deliveries per step, which the floor neither bounds nor separates, and the
floor-bound mark therefore cannot fire on the rows whose time is most dominated
by the consumer.

The header comment says the sweep over the windows in `cells/points.ts` is what
stops it (scenarios.ts:1232-1236).

card.models: A detail pane, form or per-cell component bound to specific fields of specific rows that the code already holds a handle to, with one field written per frame.
card.measures: Delivery granularity by column on pre-resolved rows: whether a write to `label` wakes only the label view and a write to `note` only the note view.
favours: Stores that route by column (per-property tracking, per-column identities): one view woken per write.

Libraries that hand back a reusable handle for a key: the address is resolved untimed in `pin` (scenarios.ts:1627-1629) and every timed write goes through it; the script's comment says the pin exists to make oimdb's identity path measurable (scenarios.ts:1516-1522).
Against row-granular stores: both views woken, one with identical text; against no-granularity stores: everything re-read.
biases: The pin is a resolution outside the clock that only some libraries can use; libraries whose id is the handle pay a keyed lookup per write. The row therefore mixes column routing with handle availability; the comment states the pin is not isolated (scenarios.ts:1531-1533).
Eight rows, off screen, window views torn down (`PINNED_COUNT`, dataset.ts:79): a constructed situation with no window derivation at all, so the row isolates delivery and nothing else.
One write per settle (scenarios.ts:1647-1661): coalescing does not enter, and `frame` is not used.

The comment cites `packages/core/src/abstract/OIMCollection.ts:469` for the lookup cost (scenarios.ts:1518); that directory does not exist in the tree (`packages/core/src/abstract/` is absent, and no `OIMCollection.ts` is under packages/core/src). The 103-132 ns versus 36-51 ns figure is unverified.
card.summary: An isolation of column-level delivery on pre-resolved rows; a real pattern for detail panes, but built around a handle some libraries do not have, so its times mix two properties.
card.body:
## What the script does

`PINNED_COUNT × 2` = 16 steps. `prepare` pins 8 off-screen rows of group A
(`pinned`, the group-A rows ranked just past the window, dataset.ts:1033) and
`pin` re-points both consumers onto them: A renders `label`, B renders `note`
(scenarios.ts:1627-1629). The first half writes each pinned label, the second
each pinned note, one settle per write (scenarios.ts:1647-1661). `restore` puts
both columns back through the same pinned path (:1633-1643). Each consumer must
produce exactly 8 distinct renders (scenarios.ts:1669-1671); the answer is in the
delivery and redundancy counters. The oracle starts from the cell state `pin`
left (`emitCells` + `settled`, :1680-1695).

## Representativeness

Per-field subscriptions on known entities are real (a selected-item inspector, a
form bound to one record, a cell component). Eight such cells is a plausible
count. The row is narrow because the window machinery is switched off and the
address resolution is taken out of the clock, which only matters for libraries
that return handles.

## The standing record, checked

Its own record (scenarios.ts:1552-1619). B4 MET (:1593-1597): `stepDeliveryOf`
returns `cell` by key (floor.ts:84) and `BOUND_BY` scales it by `cellFloor`
(floor.ts:97), whose step is one 8-line cell delivery — consistent. B1 MET
(:1573-1577) claims no participant resolves a pinned position inside the clock
while another resolves in `prepare`; that is an adapter property and is not
verified in this card.

card.models: Nothing an application does: the cell script with the store removed, used as the lower bound of the `cellDelivery` table.
card.measures: The cost of one 8-line cell delivery through `deliverCells` per step, from arrays of strings.
favours: No participant; it is the scale for the cell table. It is tight for column-routing stores (one delivery per step) and half of a row-granular store's delivery work (scenarios.ts:3743-3747).
biases: Delivers exactly one view per step (scenarios.ts:3847-3854); a correct row-granular store delivers two (one redundant). The floor therefore bounds both and separates them only through the counters.
The values are held in two prepared string arrays (scenarios.ts:3734-3735); no lookup by key and no pin is in the timed region, so it bounds the delivery and not the address.
Suffix alternation keeps every delivery distinct (scenarios.ts:3843-3844), so the digest fold is paid on every step as it is by the store rows.
card.summary: A delivery-only lower bound for the cell table; correct in shape, and its multiple is a delivery ratio, not a store ratio.
card.body:
## What the script does

16 steps in two halves. Each step writes one prepared string into
`cellFloorLabels` or `cellFloorNotes` and calls `deliverCells` (render.ts:62) on
consumer A or B (scenarios.ts:3840-3855). `check`: 8 distinct renders per
consumer and 8 lines in view B's last delivery (scenarios.ts:3856-3859). The
oracle loads the population, emits both views every step, and the digest folds
only distinct states, so both sides agree (scenarios.ts:3860-3885).

## Representativeness

An instrument, not a workload. It replaced `consumerFloor` for this table because
that floor's step is a 32-line window and overstated the bound
(scenarios.ts:3749-3752). The mapping in `floor.ts` is consistent for this pair:
`cellFloor` maps to `cell` in `FLOOR_STEP_DELIVERY` (floor.ts:52-60, at :57) and
to itself in `floorKeyFor` (floor.ts:144-147); `cellDelivery` maps to `cell` by
key (floor.ts:84) and `cell` is bound by `cellFloor` (floor.ts:97).

## The standing record, checked

Its own record (scenarios.ts:3764-3819). A3 (:3775-3779) and C5 (:3814-3818) NOT
MET are stated with reasons; both are inherent to a storeless script. B1 MET
(:3784-3788, "delivers PINNED_COUNT, which is what a store that routes by column
delivers") matches the code.

card.models: Bulk removal of everything currently visible in one list (select-all-on-page and delete, or a server purge of those keys), refilled from the rows behind.
card.measures: Batch removal from an ordered group plus the window refill, in one frame.
favours: Stores that remove a batch by one filter or rebuild pass over stores that remove element by element from a sorted array; the script was sized to stress the latter (scenarios.ts:1306-1315).
Neutral on coalescing: `remove(ids)` is ONE binding call (scenarios.ts:1337-1340), so every adapter can wrap it in its library's batch.
biases: The 32 removed rows are the lowest-ranked of group A, contiguous at the head of the sorted group (`plan.windowA`, scenarios.ts:1320, 1338; dataset.ts:794). For a splice-based ordered list that is the worst position (every remaining row shifts) and for a filter rebuild it is no different from any other; tilts against per-element splice designs. The removal in oimdb's ordered bucket is `indexOf` + `splice` (packages/core/src/engine/bucket/array/OIMBucketSlotsServiceArrayDriven.ts:58-63; `removeAt` :160-169).
The class the script's comment cites, `OIMBucketServiceOrdered` (scenarios.ts:1307-1310), does not exist in core/src; the adapter uses `OIMBucketSlotsServiceArrayDriven` (adapters/oimdb.ts:2, 138).
`repeatable: false` (scenarios.ts:1328) gives one run per sample (cells/runBatch.ts:55); the timed region is short, so per-sample noise is a larger share.
card.summary: A real bulk-delete with a refill, positioned at the head of the order; read beside `deleteOneRow`, which now measures the single-row case.
card.body:
## What the script does

One step: `remove(plan.windowA)` and `settle()` (scenarios.ts:1337-1340). A must
produce exactly one new state with a full window refilled from the next rows, B
none (scenarios.ts:1341-1350). Restore writes the deleted rows back untimed
(scenarios.ts:1333-1336). The oracle removes the same ids and emits once
(:1351-1355).

## Representativeness

Bulk delete of one page is a real UI action but rarer than deleting one row; the
row is sized to stress an ordered structure's removal path, which is a property of
one design rather than of the application (the comment says so, :1312-1314).
js-framework-benchmark's "remove row" removes ONE row from a 1000-row list; its
"clear" removes all. `deleteOneRow` (scenarios.ts:1361-1409) is now the
single-row case and `drainGroup` (:1414-1461) empties a whole group.

## The standing record, checked

`ORDINARY_SCRIPT` (scenarios.ts:86-169, signed at :95). Holds for this script.

card.models: A user deleting one visible item at a time from a sorted, paged list; js-framework-benchmark's remove row.
card.measures: One removal from an ordered group of about 200 rows, the window refilling from the row just outside it, and one full-window delivery, eight times.
favours: Stores that patch the window incrementally over those that re-derive it, and ordered buckets with cheap removal over arrays with indexOf plus splice. Each step removes one row, so the delivery of 32 lines is likely a large share; not measured for this card.
Against stores that subscribe per visible row: a removal shifts every row below it up one slot, so those stores re-point the subscriptions of the shifted rows.
biases: Removal positions are fixed: `windowA[floor(i·WINDOW/8)]` (dataset.ts:1083-1086), original positions 0, 4, …, 28. After k removals the row at original position 4k sits at current position 3k, so the current positions removed are 0, 3, 6, …, 21. The last third of the window is never removed from, and the first removal is the head.
One `remove` per step outside any `frame` (scenarios.ts:1388-1393); batching plays no part, which is the point of this row against `deleteRows`.

The removed rows are copied once in `prepare` (scenarios.ts:1375-1383) and the same objects are written back by every `restore` (:1384-1387). A store that keeps the objects it is given holds these identities across samples; whether any participant has an identity-keyed cache this warms was not checked.
card.summary: Single visible-row removal from a sorted paged list with refill, eight times; a common act at a realistic size, removing from the head and upper two-thirds of the window only.
card.body:
## What the script does

`DELETE_ONE_STEPS` = 8 (dataset.ts:207). `prepare` copies the 8 rows of
`plan.deletedOne` and builds one single-id array per step, so nothing is
allocated in the clock (scenarios.ts:1375-1383). Each step is
`remove([id])` and `settle()` (:1388-1393). `restore` writes the 8 rows back and
settles (:1384-1387). `repeatable: false` (:1374).

## What `check` and the oracle prove

`check` (scenarios.ts:1394-1401): view A distinct renders exactly 8, view B
distinct 0, final view A row count `min(WINDOW, groupSize − 8)` = 32. The oracle
removes one id and emits both views per step (:1402-1408). `finalStateOnly` is
not set, so the sequence digest and distinct counts are the criterion
(`adapterAnswer`, worker.ts:419-434), compared in both passes (verify,
worker.ts:488-531; proof in the timed process, worker.ts:644-660); the population
and grouping audits run after (worker.ts:462-464).

A store that left a short window, refilled from the wrong row, or delivered an
intermediate state (a short window, then the refill) changes the digest or
exceeds 8 distinct renders. A store that kept a removed row in its group bucket
is caught by the grouping audit where the adapter exposes one.

## Ways a broken store passes

- **Deliveries to either view are not counted**, only distinct renders; a
  redundant wake of view B is reported, not failed. That is the intended
  reading.
- Nothing found that lets a lossy removal pass: every step changes view A's
  text, and the population audit checks the end state.

## Representativeness

Removing one item from a visible sorted list is one of the most common writes a
list UI performs, and this is the store-level form of js-framework-benchmark's
"remove row" at a windowed size. Read beside `deleteRows`, which removes the
whole window in one call.

## The standing record, checked (ORDINARY_SCRIPT, scenarios.ts:86-169, signed at :96)

- A1 holds: every step must produce a new state in view A.
- B4 holds: each step delivers a full window, so `consumerFloor` (floor.ts:95)
  is a bound on it.
- B1/B2 hold as for the other ordinary scripts: both anchors have a row
  (registry.ts:33-34).

card.models: A selection refilled from nothing and then emptied under a mounted view: a folder whose items arrive and are all deleted, a cart filled and cleared.
card.measures: Inserting every row of one group into a store that holds none of them, delivering the rebuilt selection, then removing every one in one call and delivering an empty selection.
favours: Stores that derive the group's order at read time (the lean anchor rescans) over stores that keep an ordered bucket, where bucket insert or removal is linear per row. The engine's ordered bucket removes by `indexOf` plus `splice` (packages/core/src/engine/bucket/array/OIMBucketSlotsServiceArrayDriven.ts:58-63) and inserts by `splice` (:154); the scenario file's comment on `deleteRows` (scenarios.ts:1306-1310) says the same of a class name that no longer exists.

Stores with a cheap path for creating a bucket from nothing and releasing an empty one. The description's 'gives a bucket back' (scenarios.ts:1422) is phrased in the engine's terms; designs with no bucket pay nothing for it.
biases: THE REBUILT SELECTION IS NOT VERIFIED. `finalStateOnly` (scenarios.ts:1432) compares only the ending state, which is empty. A write-back that lost rows, or rendered a wrong window in step one, still produces two distinct states, an empty final view and a population and grouping audit that pass, because the removal takes every id either way. The description says so (scenarios.ts:1427-1428).

The same row objects are written in every sample: `drainRows` is cloned once in `prepare` (scenarios.ts:1434-1437) and reused by every run. A store that keeps given objects receives these exact identities again; whether any participant has an identity-keyed cache that this makes warm was not checked.
Two frames over about N/50 = 200 rows at the default point (GROUPS, dataset.ts:37). No other group is touched, so view B's silence is cheap for every design.

B4 divides by two window deliveries (`steps: 2`, scenarios.ts:1430; floor.ts:86, 95). A correct second step delivers an EMPTY window, which costs the consumer almost nothing, so the floor overstates the minimum consumer work for this script and is not a strict lower bound on it.
card.summary: A whole selection rebuilt from nothing and emptied, ending on the empty state so that the emptying is checked; the rebuild in between is checked only for having produced a state.
card.body:
## What the script does

`restore` (untimed) removes every row of group A and settles
(scenarios.ts:1438-1441), so each sample starts from a store without group A.
The run (:1442-1447) writes the rows back (`write`, keys the store no longer
holds) and settles, then removes every id in one `remove` and settles. No
`frame` call: each step is one binding call. `repeatable: true` (:1433).

## What `check` and the oracle prove

`check` (scenarios.ts:1448-1451): at least two distinct renders of view A, none
of view B, and view A left with zero rows. The oracle (:1452-1460) replays the
restore's removal, `settled()`, then the write and the removal, emitting after
each; with `finalStateOnly` the comparison is of the two views' final state
digests and row counts (worker.ts:419-447, 501-512), in both passes.

The emptying is checked three ways: view A must show no row; the population
audit (worker.ts:462) finds any row of group A a partial `remove` left; the
grouping audit (worker.ts:464) finds any id the bucket kept.

A store that skipped step one's render passes nothing: the state before the run
is empty and the consumers keep their last state between samples
(`forgetBetweenSamples` is false here, worker.ts:368-375), so a run that rendered
only the final empty state has zero distinct renders and fails `atLeast`
(scenarios.ts:416-421, 1449).

## Ways a broken store passes

- **A lossy or misordered write-back** (see biases). The script treats the
  number of states per settle as the store's answer (scenarios.ts:1426-1427),
  which is why it compares the final state only. `check` sees only the end of
  the run, so it cannot assert the rebuilt window; closing the hole needs a
  script that ends on the rebuilt state, or a model of every state a correct
  store may produce in step one.
- **The grouping audit stops at the first `undefined`.** `firstGroupingMismatch`
  returns on the first group whose `groupOrder` is `undefined`
  (oracle.ts:668-673), and group A is `g0`, the first group checked. An adapter
  that answered `undefined` for a group it holds no bucket for would skip the
  audit of all fifty groups on this script. The adapters read for this card
  answer `[]` for an absent bucket (adapters/alien-signals.ts:327,
  adapters/preact-signals.ts:283, adapters/nanostores.ts:220); not every adapter
  was read.

## Representativeness

Emptying a list under a mounted view happens, and no other script asks for an
empty selection or for a group to be rebuilt from nothing. It is narrow: two
frames, one group, values identical each time.

## The standing record, checked

`ORDINARY_SCRIPT` (scenarios.ts:86-169, signed at :103). A1 holds (two distinct
renders demanded). A3 is MET and the audits run on the emptied store, so they
say something about the removal. B4: see the floor bias above.

card.models: A page refetched or replayed with nothing changed — polling, refetch-on-focus, a websocket snapshot — written into the store as fresh objects.
card.measures: Whether the library itself detects a value-identical write and stays silent, and what the check costs.
favours: Libraries that compare values on write (per-field equality, a no-op set): no derivation, no delivery.
Against libraries that treat every write as a change (reference identity, whole-row replacement): they re-derive and deliver the identical window.
biases: No adapter may pre-filter (types.ts:11-13; scenarios.ts:1464-1466, description :1484-1486). This measures each library alone, which is fair; in applications a fetch layer often provides structural sharing before the store sees the data, so the penalty on non-comparing libraries is larger here than in apps that use such a layer.

The page is exactly view A's visible rows (`resendCopies` are clones of `windowRows`, worker.ts:164-168, 309), so every write targets a visible row — the strongest wake. A real page refetch may include rows not on screen; neutral to slight tilt against non-comparing stores.
One `write(rows)` call (scenarios.ts:1496-1502) and no `frame` call: a library can batch inside `write`, so eager and deferred stores are on equal terms without `frame`.

ADDRESSED: the window floor. `rendersNothing` is set (scenarios.ts:1489), so `stepDeliveryOf` returns `nothing` (floor.ts:79), there is no floor (floor.ts:91-100, 144-147), and the table prints `no floor` (floor.ts:191) with the `UNBOUNDED_BECAUSE` reason (floor.ts:129-136).
card.summary: A real and frequent client event — an unchanged refetch — sized to one page; it carries no floor multiple, which fits a script whose correct answer delivers nothing.
card.body:
## What the script does

One step: `write` of one of two cycled, freshly cloned copies of view A's 32 rows,
then `settle()` (scenarios.ts:1496-1502). Neither view may produce a distinct
render (scenarios.ts:1503-1505). The copies alternate so a reference check cannot
stand in for a value check (scenarios.ts:1497-1499). `restore` does nothing
(:1495); the oracle `put`s the same copy and emits once (:1506-1510).

## Representativeness

Polling and refetching unchanged data is one of the commonest client events, and
the page size is the realistic one; the earlier whole-population re-send measured
population size instead (scenarios.ts:1468-1471). js-framework-benchmark has no
equivalent; signal benchmarks test `===` equality on primitives, not row-level
value equality — `singleResend` is this suite's primitive case.

## The standing record, checked

`SILENT_SCRIPT` (scenarios.ts:171-187, signed for this key at :172). A1 NOT MET with
its reason (:175-180). B4 MET (:181-186) records that no window floor is applied;
the consumer share of a waking row is not removed, by design (floor.ts:133-135).
A `write` that silently does nothing would pass this script, as it would any
silent one; `write` is proved by the load and by the insert scripts, and the
population audit afterwards compares every stored row (worker.ts:462).

card.models: Nothing an application does: the consumer alone, driven over plain objects, used as the lower bound of every window-delivery table.
card.measures: The cost of formatting and hashing one 32-row window delivery, per step.
favours: No participant. As the divisor of the window tables it decides which rows carry the floor-bound mark (floor.ts:16, 197-203), so its accuracy tilts every one of those tables.
biases: The code still contains the per-row ternary that floor.md's tombstone (floor.md:17-30) says was removed: `i === step % rows.length ? `p${step}` : row.label` (scenarios.ts:3219), one remainder, one compare, one branch per row and one template-literal allocation per step that no participant's `deliver` performs. floor.md says this inflated the floor and deflated every multiple; it is still there.

render.md:9-10 says `consumerFloor` calls `deliver` rather than inlining it, and floor.md:25-26 says it calls `deliver` over two alternating windows; the run calls `consumer.begin/row/end` directly over `floorRows` only (scenarios.ts:3209-3223). `floorRowsB`, built for that design (worker.ts:316-319; types.ts:380-381), is used by no scenario (grep over src/).

Drives ONE consumer per step (scenarios.ts:3211) where most scripts it scales deliver to two views; floor.md:13-15 names this as an open defect. The view count and the ternary move the printed multiple in opposite directions, so 'conservative' (floor.md:9-11) is not established.

Its description says tinybase hands a pooled holder and tanstack-db an enriched row (scenarios.ts:3135-3137); floor.md:6-7 says every adapter except mobx hands plain objects. tinybase's holders are plain literals overwritten in place (adapters/tinybase.ts:80-81, 110, 158-173), so that half agrees; tanstack-db hands its live query's `toArray` with the read's virtual properties widened away by a cast (adapters/tanstack-db.ts:345-348), which is not what floor.md calls plain. Which cost is higher was not measured.
card.summary: The divisor of most tables in the report; as the code stands it is not the floor its documents describe, though it no longer divides the silent scripts.
card.body:
## What the script does

32 steps, each a delivery of the 32 rows of group A's window, built once by the
worker (worker.ts:312-315), through `BenchConsumer` with the label of one row
varied per step (scenarios.ts:3209-3223). `check`: 32 distinct renders of 32 rows
(scenarios.ts:3224-3226). The oracle re-derives the window from the population and
renders it the same way (scenarios.ts:3233-3249).

## Which tables it divides

Every scenario whose step shape resolves to `window` (`stepDeliveryOf`,
floor.ts:76-87; `BOUND_BY`, floor.ts:91-100). The four silent scripts now set
`rendersNothing: true` (scenarios.ts:501, 567, 733, 1489), which maps them to
`nothing` (floor.ts:79), a shape with no floor and a printed reason
(floor.ts:129-136). The previous card's finding that they were divided by this
floor no longer holds.

## Representativeness

An instrument. Its job is to tell a reader how much of a row is the harness's
consumer. Because every window delivery in this suite is a full re-format of 32
lines plus an FNV hash per character (consumer.ts:108-147), this number is large
relative to a single-row write, and many rows sit within a small multiple of it,
which says that the suite's consumer, not the store, dominates those rows.

## Defects to fix before the next stamp

1. Remove the ternary or restore floor.md's tombstone to the truth.
2. Either use `floorRowsB` and `deliver` as render.md and floor.md describe, or correct those documents.

## The standing record, checked

Its own record (scenarios.ts:3140-3203). B4 MET's falsifier is "this number being
subtracted rather than divided into", true of the arithmetic (`floorMultipleOf`,
floor.ts:171-181). B1 MET ("this floor rendering fewer rows or fewer lines per row
than the consumer every adapter shares") holds, but the floor performs MORE work
per step than a participant's delivery (the ternary), which B1 does not ask about.
C5 NOT MET says "every other table in the report is scaled by it" (:3197-3202);
the frame, mount and silent tables have no floor and the teardown, cell, relation
and single tables have their own (floor.ts:91-100), so that clause overstates.

card.models: Nothing an application does. It is an instrument: 256 closures pushed into one plain array, one write, every body run, one delivery, then an O(1) swap-remove of each, one more write, no delivery; eight cycles, no store and no library.
card.measures: The cost of allocating a closure, recording its position and its read in side arrays, running it once, and removing it by swap-with-tail, amortised over the largest subscriber count in the churn family.
favours: Nothing by construction: no participant runs in this table. It exists to be printed beside the churn tables.
biases: Its label (`mount lower bound`), its description and its own B4 answer call it a lower bound that scales the nine churn tables. `floor.ts` says the opposite: `BOUND_BY` has no `mount` entry (floor.ts:91-100) and `UNBOUNDED_BECAUSE` records that churn rows come out UNDER it (eight of eighteen on `churnShared`, floor.ts:108-119). A reader trusting the label is misled about every churn row's distance from it.

The per-mount bookkeeping (closure, list slot, owner and position side-array slots, a per-subscriber read slot for the churn read fold, and a swap-with-tail plus two resets to leave; scenarios.ts:3453-3480) is heavier than what a Set-based listener or a recorded-position engine pays, which is why rows beat it; the figure is a reference cost of one particular hand-written shape, not a minimum.

Amortises the two frames over 256 mounts, so its per-step frame share is the smallest in the family; comparing its per-step number to `churnOne` (one mount per two frames) compares mostly frame overhead.
card.summary: A reference cost for one hand-written mount/unmount shape with no library; despite its label it is not a lower bound and floor.ts divides no churn table by it.
card.body:
## What the script does

scenarios.ts:3450-3484: per cycle, 256 (`CHURN_SUBSCRIBERS_DEEP`, dataset.ts:146) closures are
allocated and pushed, each recording its slot, its owner and its read (:3453-3466); the root
label is written and every body runs (`mountFloorSettle`, :3328-3340); each subscriber is
swap-removed and its read cleared (:3469-3480); the label is written again and nothing is
delivered. `CHURN_CYCLES` is 8 (dataset.ts:169); `steps` is 8 × 256 (:3433). `check`
(:3490-3493) and `oracle` (:3500-3516) agree on one delivery per cycle naming 256 wakes.
`auditChurnReads: true` (:3434): on verify and proof passes the line also folds all 256 reads
(render.ts:123-141), and the oracle states each as the cycle's mark (:3512).

## Claims in the script checked against the code

- Description (scenarios.ts:3364-3372) and the blocks above it (:3273-3285, :3342-3345) say it
  is a lower bound and "the nine churn tables are scaled by this". `floor.ts:91-100`
  (`BOUND_BY`) maps `window`, `teardown`, `cell`, `relation` and `single` only;
  `floor.ts:108-119` (`UNBOUNDED_BECAUSE`, `mount`) states rows come out under it and "nothing
  here divides these rows". `floor.md:58-65` tombstones the old mapping. The description is
  stale.
- "Nine" is stale on its own terms too: `stepDeliveryOf` maps every script with `churn` set and
  not in the frame list to `mount` (floor.ts:76-81), which is the eleven `makeChurnScenario`
  scripts (scenarios.ts:2026-2690) plus `appFill` and `appRound` (`churn: 'row'`,
  scenarios.ts:2900, 2960).
- B4 MET with falsifier "a churn row coming out BELOW this number. That would mean the floor is
  not a floor" (scenarios.ts:3408-3411). By floor.ts:110-112 that has happened; by its own
  falsifier this answer is wrong. `standard.ts:443-461` accepts the MET because `mount` has an
  `UNBOUNDED_BECAUSE` entry, so the load check cannot catch it.
- The block at :3287-3290 says a row under `FLOOR_MULTIPLE_A_ROW_MUST_CLEAR` is refused a place;
  floor.md:32-37 tombstones that rule, and floor.ts now only marks (`floorBound`,
  floor.ts:197-203).
- B1 MET (:3395-3399) holds: it mounts 256 per cycle, the largest `churned` of the eleven
  `makeChurnScenario` scripts (`churnSharedDeep` and its reversal; scenarios.ts:2104, 2124).
  `churnResident` has more STANDING (256 resident plus 32 churned, :2681-2682), but mounts only
  32 per cycle.
- C5 NOT MET (:3427-3431) holds; nothing attests it.
- `SCENARIOS.md:110` repeats "Every one is scaled by `mountFloor`", also stale.

## Representativeness

Not a workload, and not claimed to be one. Its value is as a named reference number for "what
a hand-written closure list with recorded positions costs", which `WHY-EACH-ROW.md:1530-1535`
uses when it notes the anchor (`indexOf`+`splice`) does asymptotically more work than the
engine. Against public suites: js-reactivity-benchmark has no storeless reference row at all;
this one exists but is mislabelled.

## What would make it hold

Rename it to what it is (a reference cost) and change its B4/B2 answers and description to
match `floor.ts`, or rebuild it with a cheaper removal (Set delete) so it is genuinely below
every row. Either is a change outside this card's remit.

card.models: A conditional render toggling one component that subscribes to one entity: mount, the entity changes, unmount, the entity changes again with nobody listening.
card.measures: The fixed cost of creating and disposing one subscription on one source, plus two write+settle frames per pair; with one pair per two frames, the frame cost is most of each step.
favours: Stores with a cheap near-empty frame (settle with one dirty source and one or zero subscribers), since each step carries two full frames.
Stores whose subscribe allocates little (one closure or one edge) over those that build an observer object, a dependency Set or a derived atom per subscription.
biases: steps = CHURN_CYCLES × 1 = 8 (scenarios.ts:1898), so each reported step includes two writes, two settles and one delivery; the row ranks frame overhead as much as mount cost. Toward stores with low per-frame constants.

The row is resolved before the clock (`holdChurnRows` in `prepare`, scenarios.ts:1912-1918), so key-to-handle lookup is excluded from the mount for everyone. Toward identity-holding stores whose mount would otherwise start with a lookup that selector-based stores do not have.
No churn table has a floor (floor.ts:81, 91-100, 108-119), although the shared standing's B4 comment says `mountFloor` scales it (scenarios.ts:249-255).
card.summary: One subscription mounted and disposed per two frames; a real act at its smallest size, so the number is dominated by per-frame constants rather than by the mount.

## The script

Built by `makeChurnScenario` (scenarios.ts:1841-2007) with `resident: 0`,
`churned: 1`, `mount: onSharedRow` (:2026-2046, :2010). Each of `CHURN_CYCLES` = 8
(dataset.ts:169) cycles: mount subscriber 0 on `churnRows[0]` (:1936), one
`patchLabel` outside `frame` (count 1, `writeFrame`, :1880-1885) and `settle`
(:1939-1940), unmount (:1941-1945), `patchLabel` and `settle` (:1948-1949).

## What `check` and the oracle prove

`check` (:1961-1978) demands exactly one delivery and one distinct render per
cycle, silence on view B, and that the last line equals the last entry of
`deliveriesOf` (:1855-1879, last taken at :1963): woke 1, read
`CHURN_MARKS[14]` (`expectChurnHead`, :1829-1839). The line is
`churnLineOf(woke, reads)` (render.ts:140-141), with a `#1/<hash>` fold of the
one standing slot on the verify and proof passes. The oracle emits it per mounted
frame and nothing for the unmounted one (:1979-2005), compared in both passes
(worker.ts:488-534, 644-662).

The head check repeats, as an exact string, what the digest already compared line
by line; it adds a readable failure and protection against a 32-bit digest
collision on the last line, not a new constraint. At one subscriber the fold adds
little beyond the head: the standing count `1` confirms the unmount cleared the
slot's read before the next mount.

## Ways a broken store passes

- Nothing found at this size: one subscriber, one row, both frames' outcomes
  pinned. The woke count and the read are the adapter's own bookkeeping
  (render.ts:109-116), so a binding that counted a wake without the library
  calling it would be an adapter defect, outside this card.

## Representativeness

A component that appears and disappears subscribing to one entity is common (a
tooltip, a detail pane, a modal bound to the selected item). The list mount — N
components on N rows — is `churnList`.

## Standing checked against the code (CHURN_SCRIPT, scenarios.ts:202-290, listed at :204)

- A2 (:219-223) says a wake in the second frame delivers a new label that `check`
  counts as an unrequested distinct render and fails. Matches the code.
- B4 (:249-260): the comment says `floorKeyFor` hands this table `mountFloor`;
  `BOUND_BY` has no `mount` entry (floor.ts:91-100). The MET survives because
  `standard.ts:443-460` accepts a declared absence.
- B2 (:240-244): the anchor unmounts by `indexOf` plus `splice`
  (adapters/baseline-array.ts:638-650); at one subscriber that costs nothing.
- A3 NOT MET (:224-229) and C5 NOT MET (:279-288) hold as stated.

card.models: 32 components that all subscribe to the SAME entity mounting together and unmounting oldest-first, e.g. items that each read one shared record (current user, settings), torn down when a route changes.
card.measures: Per-subscriber add and remove on one source's listener list at length up to 32, plus one wake of all 32 per cycle; the per-source subscriber list structure decides it.
favours: Listener lists with O(1) removal (Set, recorded position plus swap-remove) over arrays with indexOf plus splice, though at 32 the difference is below run-to-run spread per WHY-EACH-ROW.md:1616-1619 (3.7-5.0 % of cost at 32; recorded figures, not re-measured).
Stores whose mount is one edge into an existing source list over those that build a per-subscriber observer graph.
biases: All 32 subscribers on ONE row (`onSharedRow`, scenarios.ts:2010). This is the fan-in corner; the ordinary list mount, one subscriber per row, is `churnList` (scenarios.ts:2260-2285), which also differs from this row in write volume (see that card).

The hand-written anchor unmounts with indexOf plus splice (adapters/baseline-array.ts:638-650); per WHY-EACH-ROW.md:1530-1535 and :1580-1590 `@oimdb/core` removes by recorded position (not re-read in packages/core for this card). The anchor does more work by algorithm. Toward oimdb against the anchor.
Each step includes 1/32 of two frames and one wake per subscriber per cycle, so cheap wake-up helps as much as cheap mount.
No floor divides this table (floor.ts:81, 91-100, 108-119), contrary to the standing's B4 comment (scenarios.ts:249-255).
card.summary: Mount and unmount of 32 subscribers sharing one source, oldest-first; a real but uncommon fan-in shape whose order and list-structure effects are below noise at this size.

## The script

`makeChurnScenario` (scenarios.ts:1841-2007) with `churned: CHURN_SUBSCRIBERS` = 32
(dataset.ts:143), `reversed: false` (scenarios.ts:2048-2068). Per cycle (8,
dataset.ts:169): 32 mounts on `churnRows[0]`, one `patchLabel` outside `frame`
(`writeFrame`, :1880-1885) and settle with one delivery naming 32 wakes, 32
unmounts in mount order, one write and settle with no delivery. `steps` = 8 × 32
(:1898).

## What `check` and the oracle prove

`check` (:1961-1978): deliveries and distinct both 8, view B silent, and the last
line exactly as `deliveriesOf` (:1855-1879) states it — woke 32, read
`CHURN_MARKS[14]` (`expectChurnHead`, :1829-1839) and, on the verify and proof
passes, the fold of all 32 slots' reads (render.ts:124-141). The oracle
(:1979-2005) states every line; the digest is compared in both passes
(worker.ts:488-534, 644-662).

## Ways a broken store passes

- **The woke count and the per-slot reads are the adapter's own bookkeeping**
  (render.ts:109-116); timed samples carry no fold. Subscribers 1..31 are now
  read on audited passes: a subscriber that ran and read nothing, or read the
  wrong row, changes its slot's entry in the fold.

## What decides the row

With 32 subscribers on one source, the per-source list structure and the
per-subscription allocation. WHY-EACH-ROW.md:1525 (upper bounds on a loaded
machine) recorded oimdb 126.7 ns/pair, baseline-array 73.6, jotai 516.2, and
:1616-1619 that the quadratic term is 3.7-5.0 % of cost at 32 — a linear-cost row;
the order and the quadratic are for `churnSharedDeep*`.

## Standing (CHURN_SCRIPT, scenarios.ts:202-290, listed at :205)

- A2 (:219-223) says a leaked subscriber delivers a new label that `check` fails.
  Matches the code.
- A4 (:230-234) names the per-slot read fold. Holds.
- B4 comment (:249-255) says `mountFloor` scales this table; floor.ts:91-100 says
  nothing does.
- B2 (:240-244) keeps the anchor's indexOf plus splice "because a person writing
  this writes it"; it is also why the anchor is not a lower bound here.

card.models: The same 32 components on one shared entity as `churnShared`, torn down newest-first, as a stack of routes popped or a list unmounted from the bottom.
card.measures: The cost of unmount order on a 32-long per-source listener list: for an array with indexOf plus splice, a long scan and no shift instead of a short scan and a long shift.
favours: Order-insensitive removal (Set, recorded position): those rows should equal `churnShared`; array-backed lists move.
biases: At 32 subscribers the order effect is inside run-to-run spread (WHY-EACH-ROW.md:1525-1526: oimdb 126.7 vs 132.9 ns, baseline-array 73.6 vs 80.0, with 0.3-10.7 % between-process disagreement at :1549), so the pair this row exists for is not resolved at this size. Recorded figures from before the 2026-10-17 library upgrades (jotai was 2.20.2 then, 3.0.1 is installed) and before the engine's removal changed (:1568-1590); not re-measured.
All subscribers on one row (`onSharedRow`, scenarios.ts:2010); see `churnShared`. Order only matters where a per-source list is long, which is the uncommon shape.
No floor divides this table (floor.ts:81, 91-100, 108-119), contrary to the standing's B4 comment and B4 answer (scenarios.ts:249-260).
card.summary: churnShared with LIFO unmount; it prices removal order on a 32-long listener list, an effect this suite's own run found below its noise at this size.
card.body:
## The script

Identical to `churnShared` except `reversed: true` (scenarios.ts:2070-2090), which
takes the `for (let at = last; at >= first; at--)` branch (:1941-1942). Same
`check`, head-line check and oracle (:1961-2005); see `churnShared.md` for what
they prove and what passes them.

`auditChurnReads: true` (scenarios.ts:1900): on the verify and proof passes
(worker.ts:489, 644) the churn line also folds every standing subscriber's read by
slot (`foldChurnReads`, render.ts:123-141), so a subscriber that read anything but
row 0's label fails. Timed samples skip the fold. Here every subscriber is on row 0,
so the fold proves each of the 32 read the written label, not only subscriber 0.

## What it isolates

Only the unmount order; nothing else differs between the two scripts. Whether it
matters depends on the listener structure. The anchor's indexOf plus splice
(adapters/baseline-array.ts:638-650, the scan and splice at :644-645) is
order-sensitive; `@oimdb/core` removes by a recorded position
(`unsubscribeFrom`, packages/core/src/engine/computed/OIMEffect.ts:118-126), which
is not. jotai's growth from 32 to 256 came out below 8× (WHY-EACH-ROW.md:1550),
which that file reads as an O(1) listener set; that run was on jotai 2.20.2.

## Representativeness

Both orders happen in applications, as the shape comment says
(scenarios.ts:1792-1800). The question only has an answer when many subscribers
share one source, which is the narrow case; with one subscriber per row
(`churnList`) order is irrelevant.

## Standing

Shared CHURN_SCRIPT (scenarios.ts:202-290, signed at :206). The B4 comment and
answer (:249-260) say `mountFloor` scales this table; `floorKeyFor` gives the
`mount` shape no floor (floor.ts:81, 91-100, 144-147). A2 (:219-223) now says a
leaked subscriber's delivery FAILS `check`, which matches the equality on
deliveries and distinct renders (:1961-1978); the A2 inaccuracy the previous card
carried is gone.

card.models: 256 components subscribed to one shared entity, mounted and torn down oldest-first. Rare as a workload; it is the large half of a size pair against `churnShared` to expose a quadratic unmount.
card.measures: Whether mount plus unmount on one source is linear or quadratic in the number of subscribers on it: read against churnShared, 8× growth is linear, 64× is quadratic.
favours: O(1) listener removal (Set delete, recorded position plus swap-remove). Array indexOf plus splice pays a quadratic term, recorded at 25-33 % of cost at 256 (WHY-EACH-ROW.md:1559-1566; not re-measured).
biases: The anchor keeps indexOf plus splice (adapters/baseline-array.ts:638-650) while `@oimdb/core` removes by recorded position per WHY-EACH-ROW.md:1580-1590 (not re-read in packages/core), so on this row the anchor is algorithmically handicapped against the engine. Toward oimdb in the oimdb/anchor ratio.
256 subscribers on one row (dataset.ts:146, `onSharedRow`, scenarios.ts:2010) is a stress size for a single source; ordinary lists spread subscribers over rows.
Each cycle also wakes all 256, so wake cost is in every step.
No floor divides this table (floor.ts:81, 91-100, 108-119); the `mount` reason says rows of this table come out under `mountFloor` (floor.ts:110-113).
card.summary: An instrument: 256 subscribers on one source, to show whether unmount is quadratic; read only as a ratio against churnShared, not as a workload.

## The script

`makeChurnScenario` (scenarios.ts:1841-2007) with `churned:
CHURN_SUBSCRIBERS_DEEP` = 256 (dataset.ts:146), `reversed: false`
(scenarios.ts:2092-2112). Otherwise identical to `churnShared`; the last line must
be woke 256 with read `CHURN_MARKS[14]` (`expectChurnHead`, scenarios.ts:1829-1839,
called at :1976) and, on the verify and proof passes, the fold of all 256 slots'
reads (render.ts:124-141). What the check proves and what passes it is as on
`churnShared.md`.

## The pair is the measurement

The description states it: one size cannot separate linear from quadratic
(scenarios.ts:2096-2101). That is a sound design for an instrument, and
WHY-EACH-ROW.md:1537-1566 used it to fit `F + aN + bN²` through N = 1, 32, 256.
Because it is a three-point exact interpolation there is no residual. The oimdb
`b` term priced a removal path that file says is gone (:1568-1590), so the
recorded figures do not describe the current engine.

## Representativeness

Synthetic as a workload. A 256-way fan-in on one entity exists (a global theme, a
clock) but is usually served by one subscription high in the tree. It probes
one-source fan-out on the mount/unmount side, at an unrealistic size by design.

## Standing (CHURN_SCRIPT, scenarios.ts:202-290, listed at :207)

- B2 (:240-244) deliberately keeps the anchor's O(N) removal; on this row that
  makes the anchor a weak comparison and not a lower bound.
- B4 comment (:249-255) is stale against floor.ts:91-100.
- A2 (:219-223) states that a leak fails `check`. Matches the code.

card.models: 256 subscribers on one shared entity torn down newest-first; the fourth corner of the size × order square.
card.measures: Whether an unmount-order effect grows with the number of subscribers on one source (array indexOf plus splice) or is constant (Set, recorded position).
favours: Order-insensitive O(1) removal; array-backed lists pay the long scan on every unmount.
biases: Same anchor asymmetry as churnSharedDeep: anchor indexOf plus splice (adapters/baseline-array.ts:638-650) against the engine's positional removal (`unsubscribeFrom`, packages/core/src/engine/computed/OIMEffect.ts:118-126). Toward oimdb in that ratio.
Stress size on a single source (dataset.ts:146); one subscriber per row (`churnList`) has no order effect at all.
No floor divides this table (floor.ts:81, 91-100, 108-119).
card.summary: An instrument completing the size × order square for unmount on one source; meaningful only as a ratio against its three siblings.
