## The script

`reversed: true`, `churned: 256` (scenarios.ts:2114-2132); LIFO branch at
:1941-1942. Same check, head-line check and oracle as the other row-shape scripts
(:1961-2005); see `churnShared.md`. `auditChurnReads: true` (:1900): on verify and
proof passes (worker.ts:489, 644) all 256 standing reads are folded by slot into
the churn line (render.ts:123-141), so each subscriber must have read row 0.

## What it adds

With `churnShared`, `churnSharedReversed` and `churnSharedDeep`, it lets a reader
see whether the order gap at 32 grows at 256. WHY-EACH-ROW.md:1527-1528 recorded
oimdb 146.5 → 164.8 ns and baseline-array 83.6 → 97.1 ns going to newest-first at
256, against near-equal pairs at 32; those were on a loaded machine, on jotai
2.20.2 (3.0.1 is installed), and the engine's removal has since changed
(:1568-1590).

## Representativeness

As for `churnSharedDeep`: an isolation, not a workload. Its weight for an
application is small, because the long single-source list is the uncommon shape.

## Standing

Shared CHURN_SCRIPT (scenarios.ts:202-290, signed at :208). The B4 comment and
answer (:249-260) still say `mountFloor` scales this table, against floor.ts:91-100.
A2 (:219-223) now states that a leaked subscriber fails `check`, which is what the
check does (:1961-1978); that inaccuracy is gone.

card.models: One component that reads 64 entities at once (a summary, a total, a chart over a selection) mounting and unmounting.
card.measures: What a subscription pays for a 64-entry source list: registering in 64 sources on mount and leaving each on unmount, plus any deduplication or expansion of the list.
favours: Stores whose multi-source subscribe is one object plus one edge per source (an effect over a source array, a hand-written list per id) over stores that compose a derived node over 64 per-entity nodes.
Stores that take the source list as given; the script never asks a store to discover its sources by tracking reads, so tracking-based designs pay for a capability the script does not exercise.
biases: The source list is static and known at mount (`mountOnRows(at, 0, CHURN_WIDE)`, scenarios.ts:2149). No dynamic dependencies: a component whose reads change between renders is not represented. Toward explicit-source designs.
The 64 rows are resolved before the clock (`holdChurnRows` in `prepare`, scenarios.ts:1912-1918), so the lookup of 64 keys is excluded from every mount.
One subscriber per cycle, so per step = one 64-source pair plus two frames; the frame share is small relative to 64 registrations but still present.
No floor divides this table (floor.ts:81, 91-100, 108-119).
card.summary: One subscriber over 64 statically known sources mounted and disposed; real for aggregate components, blind to dynamic dependency tracking, and its check proves registration on one source only.

## The script

`makeChurnScenario` with `wiring: 'wide'`, `churned: 1`,
`mount: (churn, at) => churn.mountOnRows(at, 0, CHURN_WIDE)`
(scenarios.ts:2134-2155), `CHURN_WIDE` = 64 (dataset.ts:149). The write lands on
`churnRows[0]` only (`churnRowOnly`, scenarios.ts:2014; `writeFrame` with one row
calls `patchLabel(ids[0], …)`, :1880-1885).

## What `check` and the oracle prove

`check` (:1961-1978): 8 deliveries, 8 distinct, view B silent, last line
`expectChurnHead` (:1829-1840), i.e. `1:${CHURN_MARKS[14]}` plus, on verify and
proof passes, the read fold `#1/<hash>` (`churnLineOf`, render.ts:140-141). The
oracle (:1979-2005) states every line, compared in both passes (worker.ts:488-492
with the runner's digest comparison of the emitted `digestA`/`oracleA`;
worker.ts:644-660 in the timed process).

## Ways a broken store passes

- **Registration on 63 of the 64 sources is never tested.** Only row 0 is written,
  so a store or binding that registered on the first source only passes `check`,
  the digest and the head check, and posts a faster time. The churn read fold
  (`auditChurnReads`, scenarios.ts:1900; render.ts:123-141) does not close this:
  it folds one read per standing SUBSCRIBER, and the one subscriber here reports
  row 0's label (`rowOf: onRowZero`, `headOf: asRead`, :2153-2154; the anchor's
  `readInto(at, first)`, adapters/baseline-array.ts:579-581). Whether any adapter
  registers on fewer than 64 sources was not verified here; the population audit
  cannot see it, because no subscription state is audited.
- **A leaked registration on sources 1..63 is never tested either**: the unmounted
  frame writes row 0 only, so a subscriber that left row 0 but stayed on the
  others delivers nothing and passes.

## What decides the row

The cost per source of registering and leaving. WHY-EACH-ROW.md:1637-1641 (upper
bounds, loaded machine) recorded oimdb 65.4 ns/source, baseline-array 46.4,
jotai 1025, with the note that jotai's derived atom over 64 atoms is a different
object graph. That run was on jotai 2.20.2; 3.0.1 is installed. Not re-measured.

## Representativeness

An aggregate component over a selection exists in applications. What applications
also do and this cannot ask: a subscription whose source set changes between runs
(conditional reads). Here the set is fixed at mount.

## Standing (CHURN_SCRIPT, scenarios.ts:202-290, signed at :209)

- A1 MET (:213-218) proves liveness on one source, and its fold of "what EVERY
  standing subscriber read" is one read here, not 64; the falsifier is narrower
  than the description's claim to price "registering in each source"
  (scenarios.ts:2142-2143).
- B4 comment and answer (:249-260) say `mountFloor` scales this table; floor.ts:91-100
  gives the `mount` shape no floor. A2 (:219-223) now matches `check`.

card.models: 32 components that each read one FIELD (`label`) of one shared entity, as a field-level selector or signal, mounting together and unmounting oldest-first.
card.measures: The difference between subscribing to a column identity and to a whole row, at the same count, root and order as churnShared: minting or finding the column handle and releasing it.
favours: Stores with a first-class field identity (field signals, column handles) over stores that model a field subscription as a selector with an equality check.
Stores that mint the column handle cheaply and share it across the 32 subscribers.
biases: Two libraries decline: lokijs (adapters/lokijs.ts:472, reason at :1010-1017) and redux-toolkit (adapters/redux-toolkit.ts:547, reason at :1137-1144), as do `baseline-array-indexed` (adapters/baseline-array-indexed.ts:405) and `control-write` (harness/control.ts:1258). This table and churnShared hold different populations; the pair comparison is across two populations for those rows.

The hand-written anchor keeps a second Map of `label` subscribers by row id (adapters/baseline-array.ts:431-432, mount at :583-588) and its settle probes both maps for every touched row (adapters/baseline-array.ts:531-543). That probe is paid on every churn script, not only here. WHY-EACH-ROW.md:1627-1636 recorded the anchor at 174.6 vs 73.6 ns/pair and attributes it to a `${id}|label` key the current anchor no longer builds; that figure describes an older anchor body.

Only `label` is written, and every subscriber reads `label`; nothing measures whether a column subscription stays silent when ANOTHER column of the row changes, which is the point of subscribing to a column.
All 32 on one row (`mountOnColumn` reads `churnRows[0]`, e.g. adapters/oimdb.ts:489-495); see churnShared.
No floor divides this table: `stepDeliveryOf` returns `mount` (floor.ts:81), `BOUND_BY` has no `mount` entry (floor.ts:91-100), `UNBOUNDED_BECAUSE` gives the reason (floor.ts:108-119).
card.summary: Mount and unmount of 32 field-level subscriptions on one row; read only against churnShared, with two libraries absent from this table, and no frame that shows the payoff of column addressing.

## The script

`makeChurnScenario` (scenarios.ts:1841-2007) with `wiring: 'column'`,
`churned: 32`, `mount: (churn, at) => churn.mountOnColumn(at)`
(scenarios.ts:2157-2258, mount at :2252). Same cycle, check, head-line check and
oracle as the row shape (:1930-2005); the last line must be
`churnLineOf(32, reads)` with every slot reading `CHURN_MARKS[14]`, folded by slot
on the verify and proof passes (render.ts:124-141). What passes it is as on
`churnShared.md`.

## Representativeness

Field-level subscriptions are what a selector-based app does on almost every
component, so the act is ordinary. Narrow: all 32 on one row, and no frame writes
a different column, so the row prices the cost of column addressing without its
payoff.

## Standing (own record, scenarios.ts:2183-2248)

- The comment above the record (scenarios.ts:2170-2182) says the per-shape split
  took `lokijs` and `oimdb-3.12.1` out of this table. `oimdb-legacy` (version
  3.12.1) implements `mountOnColumn` (adapters/oimdb-legacy.ts:444), and
  redux-toolkit, which the comment does not name, declines it. The comment is
  stale on both names.
- A4 MET (:2199-2203) names the per-slot read fold.
- B1 MET (:2204-2208) holds for the declines read: they throw (`declinedMount`,
  types.ts:130-137) rather than subscribe to the row.
- B3 MET (:2214-2218) names LokiJS; redux-toolkit declines for the same reason
  (adapters/redux-toolkit.ts:1137-1144). Holds for the adapter read
  (adapters/oimdb.ts:489-495 uses `channel.effectOnColumn(rows.holdColumn(…))`);
  others not read for this card.
- B4 MET (:2219-2222): no floor divides this table, so B4's demand is not met in
  substance; the MET passes only the declared-absence check (standard.ts:443-460).

card.models: A list of 32 items mounting one component per row, a batch of those rows updating, then the list unmounting: the ordinary list mount.
card.measures: 32 single-row subscriptions on 32 distinct rows mounted and disposed per cycle, plus a frame that writes 4 to 32 of those rows inside `frame` before and after the unmount.
favours: Stores with a per-row subscriber list: each list has length one, so list structure (array, Set, position) stops mattering and the per-subscription allocation decides.

Libraries whose batching API `frame` reaches (scenarios.ts:1886-1889): up to 32 writes per frame become one notification. Redux Toolkit's adapter defers listeners to the frame end with autoBatch (adapters/redux-toolkit.ts:72-101), but each of its 32 subscriber selectors still runs once per frame.
Against stores with one store-wide listener: every standing subscriber's selector runs on each notification, written row or not (adapters/redux-toolkit.ts:449-462).
biases: THE PAIR WITH `churnShared` IS NOT ISOLATED. The description says the gap against `churnShared` is what a subscriber list per row costs (scenarios.ts:2272-2274). The scripts also differ in write volume: this one writes 32+28+…+4 = 144 rows twice per run, 288 `patchLabel` calls inside `frame` (`churnListPrefix`, scenarios.ts:2020-2022; `writeFrame`, :1880-1890), where `churnShared` writes 16 calls outside any `frame`. The gap includes 272 extra writes and 16 frame scopes.
32 rows is a small list; js-framework-benchmark-style list mounts are 1000 rows. The mount count per cycle is the same as `churnShared`'s, by design.
The rows are resolved before the clock (`holdChurnRows`, scenarios.ts:1912-1918), so key lookup is out of every mount.
No floor divides this table: `stepDeliveryOf` returns `mount` (floor.ts:81), `BOUND_BY` has no `mount` entry (floor.ts:91-100), `UNBOUNDED_BECAUSE` gives the reason (floor.ts:108-119).
card.summary: One subscription per row for a 32-row list, mounted, written and torn down; the ordinary list shape at a small size, whose gap against the shared-root row also carries 272 extra writes.

## What the script does

`makeChurnScenario` (scenarios.ts:1841-2007) with `wiring: 'row'`,
`churned: 32`, `mount: (churn, at) => churn.mountOnRows(at, at, 1)` — subscriber
`i` on churn row `i` (scenarios.ts:2260-2285, mount at :2279). `rowsWrittenIn`
and `wokeIn` are both `churnListPrefix` (:2022): 32 − 4·cycle, so 32, 28, …, 4
across the 8 cycles (`CHURN_LIST_SHRINK` = 4, :2020). Each mounted frame writes
that prefix inside `frame` with labels `${mark}.${row}` (row 0 gets the bare mark,
`churnLabelOf`, :1810-1815; `writeFrame`, :1886-1889) and settles; the unmounted
frame writes the same prefix with the next mark. `restore` writes the 32 rows back
(:1922-1929).

## What `check` and the oracle prove

`check` (:1961-1978): 8 deliveries, 8 distinct, nothing on view B, and the last
line as `deliveriesOf` (:1855-1879) states it — woke 4, row 0's read
`CHURN_MARKS[14]`, and on the verify and proof passes the fold of all 32 slots'
reads, slot `i` reading row `i`'s label (`rowOf: at => at`, :2283;
render.ts:124-141). The oracle (:1979-2005) names the prefix length as the woke
count in every mounted frame, and the digest is compared in both passes
(worker.ts:488-534, 644-662).

Misplacement fails in every direction on the audited passes: all 32 on row 0 name
32 in every cycle; subscriber `i` on row `i+1` names `prefix − 1`; and any
permutation of subscribers among rows, including inside a block of four where the
count is unchanged, puts a different label under a slot index and changes the
fold.

## Ways a broken store passes

- **The woke count and the per-slot reads are the adapter's own bookkeeping**
  (render.ts:109-116); timed samples carry no fold.

## Representativeness

This is one component per row — what list rendering does on navigation.
Representative, at the size of a small page; read the comparison with
`churnShared` with the write-volume difference in mind.

## The standing record, checked (CHURN_SCRIPT, scenarios.ts:202-290, listed at :210)

- A2 (:219-223) says a wake in the second frame delivers a new label, which
  `check` counts as an unrequested distinct render and fails. Matches the code.
- A4 (:230-234) names the per-slot read fold and a subscriber on the wrong row.
  Holds.
- B4 comment (:249-255) says `floorKeyFor` hands this table `mountFloor`; it hands
  it none (floor.ts:91-100). The B4 falsifier itself (:256-260) is not triggered.

card.models: 32 components each building its own selector stack at mount (a selector factory, per-instance derived atoms or computeds) of 4 derivations over 8 entities, then torn down.
card.measures: Building and tearing down a 4-deep linear derivation chain per subscriber, including whatever walk the store does to find the roots under the chain.
favours: Hand-written code, which knows the roots statically and builds nothing at mount (adapters/baseline-array.ts:589-618); the standing admits the two sides do not do the same job (B1 NOT MET, scenarios.ts:2326-2334).
Stores whose derived nodes are cheap to allocate and whose subscription does not expand roots through the chain.
biases: The chain is linear: level k applies `chainLevelOf` to level k−1 (derivations.ts:1-7; e.g. adapters/oimdb.ts:496-527, adapters/mobx.ts:415-429, adapters/redux-toolkit.ts:548-558). No diamond (that is `churnDiamond`), no fan-in between derivations, no equality cutoff exercised (every write changes root 0 and so every level), no derivation shared between the 32 subscribers.
Depth 4 (dataset.ts:162) is shallow; a store with O(depth) per-level overhead is hard to separate from one with O(1).

All 32 subscribers build identical chains over the same 8 rows (scenarios.ts:2378-2379); in applications such selectors are often memoised once and shared. Toward cheap per-instance allocation, against stores that would share.
The mount comparison against the anchor is not comparable (B1 NOT MET), and the report prints no per-row note for it, by the standing's own text.

Population: signaldb and lokijs decline the chain (adapters/signaldb.ts:1175-1180, adapters/lokijs.ts:1018-1024), as do `baseline-array-indexed` (adapters/baseline-array-indexed.ts:405) and `control-write` (harness/control.ts:1258).
No floor divides this table: `stepDeliveryOf` returns `mount` (floor.ts:81), `BOUND_BY` has no `mount` entry (floor.ts:91-100), and `UNBOUNDED_BECAUSE` gives the reason (floor.ts:108-119).
card.summary: Per-subscriber linear selector stacks built and destroyed; it prices mount-time chain construction, with every chain's depth checked on audited passes, but no graph shape (sharing, cutoff) that differentiates reactive engines.

## The script

`makeChurnScenario` (scenarios.ts:1841-2007) with `wiring: 'chain'`,
`churned: 32`,
`mount: (churn, at) => churn.mountOnChain(at, 0, CHURN_CHAIN_ROOTS, CHURN_CHAIN_DEPTH)`,
`headOf: chainHead` (scenarios.ts:2287-2385, `chainHead` at :2024), 8 roots and
depth 4 (dataset.ts:161-162). The write lands on the first root (`churnRowOnly`,
:2014) as one `patchLabel` outside `frame` (`writeFrame`, :1880-1885).

## What `check` and the oracle prove

`deliveriesOf` (scenarios.ts:1855-1879) states each mounted frame's line: woke 32
and every standing slot's read, `chainHeadOf(label, 4)` = `${label}>1>2>3>4`
(derivations.ts:3-7). `check` (:1961-1978) compares the last line exactly
(`expectChurnHead`, :1829-1839); the oracle (:1979-2005) emits every line. On the
verify and proof passes the line folds all 32 slots' reads (render.ts:124-141), so
a subscriber that built fewer levels, or skipped a level's recomputation, renders
a shorter text in its slot and fails — any of the 32, not only subscriber 0.

## Ways a broken store passes

- **The four levels are not observable as nodes.** The text is the same whether
  four library nodes compose it or one function applies `chainLevelOf` four times;
  the latter is what the anchor does (adapters/baseline-array.ts:602-610). An
  adapter that folded the levels would pass. B2/B3 forbid it
  (scenarios.ts:2335-2344); `check` cannot see it.
- **Only root 0 is written**, so registration on roots 1..7 is untested, as on
  `churnWide`.
- The woke count and the per-slot reads are the adapter's own bookkeeping
  (render.ts:109-116); timed samples carry no fold.

## What decides the row

Allocation of 4 derived nodes per subscriber and the root walk at subscribe.
WHY-EACH-ROW.md:1642-1650 recorded oimdb 797.2 ns/pair vs 126.7 for a flat mount,
and baseline-array 639.6 paid "depth × count reads per wake-up". The anchor's body
now reads the 8 roots once and applies the 4 levels to the result
(adapters/baseline-array.ts:602-610), so that description of the anchor is
out of date.

## Representativeness

Per-component derived state built at mount is real (hooks creating computeds,
`atom()` inside a component). The narrowness is the graph: a single linear chain,
never shared, never cut off.

## Standing (own record, scenarios.ts:2303-2374)

- A4 MET (:2319-2325) holds for every standing slot: the head text is in the read
  fold, compared in the verify pass and in the timed process's proof pass
  (worker.ts:488-534, 644-662).
- B1 NOT MET (:2326-2334) is accurate and is the largest caveat on the row.
- B2 MET (:2335-2339): the anchor derives 4 levels per wake over one read of the
  roots, so the frame derives the same number of levels as the engine. Holds.
- B4 MET (:2347-2350) and the comment above it (:2345-2346, "this table is scaled
  by `mountFloor`") are stale against floor.ts:91-100: no floor scales this table.

card.models: A screen of 32 mounted components, each with its own stack of 4 derived values over 8 entities, receiving one write to an entity they all read, frame after frame.
card.measures: Propagating one root write through 32 standing linear derivation chains and running every subscriber body once — the run half of `churnChain`, with mounting outside the clock.
favours: Engines whose derived nodes are cheap to re-evaluate: each level of the oimdb wiring is an `OIMSingleComputed` applying `chainLevelOf` to the level below (adapters/oimdb.ts:525-545).

The hand-written anchor reads the 8 roots once per wake and applies the 4 levels in one body (adapters/baseline-array.ts:594-618, `derive` at :602-610); it re-evaluates nothing it did not need, so it is a fair lower reference for the frame.
biases: Every write changes root 0's label (CHURN_MARKS, scenarios.ts:1735-1738), so every level's value changes and no equality cutoff is exercised; no diamond (that is `churnDiamond`), no fan-in between derivations, and the 32 chains are built separately over the same 8 roots, so a store that would share them gets no credit.
Depth 4 over 8 roots (dataset.ts:161-162) is shallow; O(1) and O(depth) per-level overheads are hard to separate here.
The consumer receives one line per step (`deliverChurn`, render.ts:143-153), so the consumer's share of the time is small and the row is mostly store work. No floor divides it (see standing).
Each step is one `patchLabel` outside `frame` (scenarios.ts:2481-2487), so batching plays no part.

Population: signaldb and lokijs decline the chain (adapters/signaldb.ts:1175-1180, adapters/lokijs.ts:1018-1024), as do `baseline-array-indexed` (no churn wiring, adapters/baseline-array-indexed.ts:405) and `control-write` (harness/control.ts:1258).
card.summary: Propagation through standing per-component selector stacks, isolated from mounting; real in kind but linear, unshared and shallow, and the full depth of every chain is checked on audited passes.

## What the script does

`prepare` mounts `CHURN_SUBSCRIBERS` = 32 chains of depth 4 over 8 roots, untimed
(scenarios.ts:2468-2474). The run is `CHURN_MARKS.length` = 16 steps, each a
`patchLabel` on root 0 and a `settle` (:2481-2487). `restore` puts root 0's label
back (:2475-2480). `auditChurnReads: true` (:2465).

## What `check` and the oracle prove

`check` (scenarios.ts:2488-2496): 16 deliveries, 16 distinct, nothing on view B,
and the last line exactly
`churnLineOf(32, chainFrameReadsOf(CHURN_MARKS[15]))` (`expectChurnHead`,
:1829-1839). `chainFrameReadsOf` (:2387-2388) is 32 copies of
`chainHeadOf(mark, 4)`, so on the verify and proof passes the line folds every
standing chain's head by slot (render.ts:124-141). The oracle (:2497-2504) emits
the same line per step; compared in the verify pass (worker.ts:488-534) and the
proof pass (worker.ts:644-662). `chainHeadOf` appends `>1>2>3>4`
(derivations.ts:3-7), so any of the 32 chains that built fewer levels, or did not
re-derive, renders a different text in its slot and fails.

## Ways a broken store passes

- **Levels folded into fewer nodes render the same text** (see `churnChain.md`).
  B2/B3 (scenarios.ts:2426-2434) forbid it; `check` cannot see it.
- **The woke count and the per-slot reads are the adapter's own bookkeeping**
  (render.ts:109-116); timed samples carry no fold.

## Representativeness

Per-component derived state that stays mounted while data changes is the normal
case with selector hooks or computed props; pairing this row with `churnChain`
separates build cost from run cost. Narrow: one unshared line with no cutoff.

## The standing record, checked (scenarios.ts:2401-2462)

- A3 NOT MET (:2410-2414) agrees with standard.ts (a churn wiring is not auditable
  by grouping).
- A4 MET (:2415-2420) now names the per-slot read fold and holds for all 32 chains.
- B1 MET (:2421-2425) holds: both sides mount in `prepare`.
- B4 MET (:2435-2439): `chainFrameWrite` is in `STANDING_FRAME_SCENARIO_KEYS`
  (floor.ts:69-72), `stepDeliveryOf` returns `frame` (floor.ts:80), and
  `UNBOUNDED_BECAUSE` gives the `frame` reason (floor.ts:120-128): a step mounts
  nothing and is one write, the bodies that read it and one line. That describes
  this script.
- C5 NOT MET (:2456-2461) agrees with `control-write` declining churn
  (harness/control.ts:1258).

card.models: 32 components each building, at mount, two derived values from one shared entity and a third that combines them, then torn down; the combined value must update once per change.
card.measures: Building and disposing three derived nodes and one subscription per component over one shared root, plus one propagation through 32 diamonds per cycle, with a glitch (the join running once per arm) turned into a failure rather than a time.
favours: Hand-written code, which computes both arms and the join inline in one body and builds no graph (adapters/baseline-array.ts:619-637); the standing says the mount is not comparable (B1 NOT MET, scenarios.ts:2541-2548).
Libraries whose derived nodes are cheap to allocate and to dispose. Every passing library is glitch-free on this graph, so the time ranks graph construction and teardown, not scheduling.

Pull-based or topologically ordered designs pass the correctness gate for nothing (mobx computeds, adapters/mobx.ts:430-436; reselect, adapters/redux-toolkit.ts:559-570); a push design without ordering fails instead of ranking.
biases: ONE SHARED ROOT. Every diamond is over `churnRows[0]` (`mountOnDiamond(at, 0)`, scenarios.ts:2587), so a store where each arm subscribes to the root puts 64 arm subscriptions on one source list. List-structure costs of `churnShared` (indexOf plus splice) are mixed into this row.
The 32 diamonds are identical and never shared; a store that would dedupe identical derivations gets no credit, and one with cheap per-instance allocation is favoured.
The only write is one `patchLabel` per frame outside `frame` (`writeFrame` with count 1, scenarios.ts:1880-1885), so batching plays no part.
No floor divides this table: `stepDeliveryOf` returns `mount` (floor.ts:81), `BOUND_BY` has no `mount` entry (floor.ts:91-100) and `UNBOUNDED_BECAUSE` gives the reason (floor.ts:108-119).

Population differs from the row shape: signaldb and lokijs decline the diamond (adapters/signaldb.ts:1181-1186, adapters/lokijs.ts:1025-1031), as do `baseline-array-indexed` (adapters/baseline-array-indexed.ts:405) and `control-write` (harness/control.ts:1258).
card.summary: A per-component diamond built and destroyed at mount, gated on glitch-freedom; the time prices three derived nodes per subscriber over one shared root, and every standing diamond's joined text is checked on audited passes.

## What the script does

`makeChurnScenario` (scenarios.ts:1841-2007) with `wiring: 'diamond'`,
`churned: CHURN_SUBSCRIBERS` = 32 (dataset.ts:143), `reversed: false`,
`headOf: diamondHeadOf` (scenarios.ts:2507-2593). Each of `CHURN_CYCLES` = 8
cycles (dataset.ts:169) mounts 32 diamonds on row 0 (:1936), writes row 0's label
and settles (:1939-1940), unmounts oldest-first (:1941-1945), writes again and
settles (:1948-1949). `steps` = 8 × 32 (:1898).

`diamondHeadOf(label)` is `${label}<|>${label}` (derivations.ts:9-15), so the
delivered line (`churnLineOf`, render.ts:140-141) must read `32:s…<|>s…` in each
mounted frame, followed on the verify and proof passes by the fold of all 32
slots' joined text (render.ts:124-138).

## What `check` and the oracle prove

`check` (scenarios.ts:1961-1978) demands 8 deliveries, 8 distinct renders, none on
view B, and that the last line equals the one `deliveriesOf` (:1855-1879) states
for the last mounted frame (`expectChurnHead`, :1829-1839). The oracle
(:1979-2005) emits one line per mounted frame and nothing for an unmounted one;
the sequence digest is compared in the verify pass and again in the timed
process's proof pass (worker.ts:488-534, 644-662).

A glitch fails: the adapters count a wake each time the subscriber body runs
(e.g. adapters/mobx.ts:286-296, adapters/redux-toolkit.ts:449-462), so a join
that re-ran after each arm and re-ran the subscriber names 64, and an
inconsistent read (`new<|>old`) left as any slot's last value changes the fold.

## Ways a broken store passes

- **The three nodes are not observable.** The text is identical whether the arms
  and join are three library nodes or one function; an adapter that folded them
  would pass and post the anchor's shape. That is B2/B3's promise
  (scenarios.ts:2549-2556), not something `check` can see.
- **The woke count and the per-slot reads are the adapter's own bookkeeping**
  (render.ts:109-116). An adapter whose wake counter ignored a second body run
  would hide a glitch. Timed samples carry no fold.
- A glitch whose extra join run does not re-run the subscriber (the library
  suppresses an unchanged join) is invisible, and harmless.

## Representativeness

A component deriving two values from one prop and combining them is ordinary; the
diamond is the smallest graph where glitch-freedom matters, which
js-reactivity-benchmark-style suites probe on propagation. Here it is probed at
mount and teardown, at depth one, with every arm reading the same row. Narrow:
read against `churnChain` (a line) and `churnShared` (no derivation).

## The standing record, checked (scenarios.ts:2522-2583)

- A4 MET (:2536-2540) holds: every standing slot's joined text and the woke count
  are compared in the timed process too (worker.ts:644-662).
- B1 NOT MET (:2541-2548) holds; the anchor's body also keeps a per-settle guard
  (`ranAtSettle`, adapters/baseline-array.ts:623, 628-630) that no library-side
  wiring is allowed (B3, :2553-2556). On this script row 0 is touched once per
  frame, so the guard does not change the anchor's count; it is still the anchor
  doing deduplication by hand.
- B4 MET (:2557-2560) passes the load check through the declared `mount` absence
  (standard.ts:443-460).
- C5 NOT MET (:2577-2582) agrees with `control-write` declining churn
  (harness/control.ts:1258).

card.models: A screen that keeps most of its subscriptions and churns a fraction: 256 standing subscribers on one entity, 32 more mounted and unmounted on it per cycle.
card.measures: End-to-end churn against a long standing listener list on one source: 32 mounts and unmounts plus 288 + 256 wakes per cycle, not mount cost alone.
favours: Stores with cheap wake-up per subscriber: per cycle 544 bodies run where churnShared runs 32 (WHY-EACH-ROW.md:1651-1660), so wake cost dominates the time.
Stores whose unmount is O(1) in the standing list (Set, recorded position); indexOf plus splice scans up to 288 entries per unmount.
biases: The residents share the churned root (`mountResident: onSharedRow`, scenarios.ts:2683), so both frames wake them; the row cannot separate mount cost from wake cost (A1 NOT MET, scenarios.ts:2612-2620). A reader using it as 'mount cost when 256 are standing' reads the wrong number.

In an application the standing subscriptions of a screen sit on many entities, so a churned mount does not lengthen any one list; putting all 288 on one source makes list length the variable, which is the uncommon case.
Per step (`steps` = 8 × 32, scenarios.ts:1898) carries 17 wakes plus a share of two frames. Toward stores with fast notification loops.

Anchor uses indexOf plus splice (adapters/baseline-array.ts:638-650) while the engine removes by recorded position per WHY-EACH-ROW.md:1580-1590 (not re-read in packages/core); toward oimdb in that ratio.
No floor divides this table (floor.ts:81, 91-100, 108-119).
card.summary: Churn of 32 subscribers against 256 standing ones on the same source; an end-to-end churn-plus-notify cost, dominated by resident wake-ups, not a mount cost under load.

## The script

`makeChurnScenario` (scenarios.ts:1841-2007) with `resident: CHURN_RESIDENT` =
256, `churned: CHURN_CHURNED` = 32 (dataset.ts:157-158, scenarios.ts:2595-2690).
Residents take indices 0..255 and mount in `prepare`, untimed (:1912-1918); the
churned take 256..287 (:1932-1933). Both frames deliver (`deliveriesPerCycle` = 2,
:1843): the first names 288, the second 256, which proves the churned 32 left
(`deliveriesOf`, :1874-1876; oracle, :2000-2003).

## What `check` and the oracle prove

`check` (:1961-1978): 16 deliveries, 16 distinct, view B silent, and the last line
as `deliveriesOf` states it — for this script the last delivering frame is the
unmounted one, so woke 256, read `CHURN_MARKS[15]`, and on the verify and proof
passes the fold of the 256 resident slots (render.ts:124-141). A churned
subscriber that did not leave names 257 or more and, because its read was not
cleared, adds a slot to the fold's standing count; either fails.

## Ways a broken store passes

- **The woke count and the per-slot reads are the adapter's own bookkeeping**
  (render.ts:109-116); timed samples carry no fold. Every resident and churned
  slot's read is in the fold on audited passes, so residents 1..255 and the
  churned 32 are no longer attested by the count alone.

## Representativeness

The motivation (scenarios.ts:2599-2608) is sound: a screen churns a fraction. The
construction does not model it: the standing population of a real screen is
spread over many entities. What this row does show is the cost of notifying a long
list while it is being edited.

## Standing (own record, scenarios.ts:2611-2680)

- A1 NOT MET (:2612-2620) is accurate and should be read first.
- A2 MET (:2621-2625) holds: the second frame must name the resident count, and
  its read fold must hold no churned slot.
- A4 MET (:2631-2635) names the per-slot read fold.
- B2 MET (:2641-2645) keeps the anchor's linear unmount; on this row that is where
  it is most expensive.
- B4 MET (:2653-2656) and the comment above it (:2651-2652) say this table is
  scaled by `mountFloor`; floor.ts:91-100 gives it no floor.

card.models: A screen opening: 180 components mount over 80 cards, 10 decks and 5 users, and part of the data they show changes in the same frame.
card.measures: Mounting 180 single-row subscriptions inside the clock, then one frame of 46 label writes that must wake exactly the 87 subscribers whose own row was written, delivered as one line.
favours: Stores whose per-subscription mount is cheap; 180 mounts against 46 writes make the mount the larger share of the step.

Libraries whose batching API `frame` reaches (scenarios.ts:2916-2921) pay one notification instead of 46. The wake count does not change with batching: every subscriber reads one row (`mountOnRows(…, 1)`, scenarios.ts:2749-2753), and each written row is written once.
Against stores with one store-wide listener: every standing subscriber's selector runs at the notification, written row or not (adapters/redux-toolkit.ts:449-462).
biases: Nothing is inserted. The 95 scene rows are the first 95 rows of the dataset (`holdAppScene`, scenarios.ts:2726-2734), already in the store from the load (worker.ts:342-353, called at :362); the frame PATCHES labels. A screen fill usually creates rows as components mount, so key-creation cost is not in this row.

The three entity kinds are names, not types: cards, decks and users are rows of one collection with one shape, distinguished only by index offsets (scenarios.ts:2692-2700). A deck's date subscriber reads a fixed user row chosen by the harness (`appUserOfDeck`, :2700), so no relation is resolved by the store.
Each card has two subscribers on the same row (card and tag 0, scenarios.ts:2739-2742), so the fan-in is two per card, one per deck name and two per user.
One frame, 46 writes, 180 subscribers: a small screen. Mount and write are not separated, so a row's time cannot be split between them from this table alone.
card.summary: Mount wave plus one partial write frame over a small single-collection scene; the woke count and, on audited passes, the per-slot read fold say which row every subscriber sits on.
card.body:
## What the script does

`prepare` resolves the 95 scene rows (scenarios.ts:2904-2906). The run
(:2913-2923) mounts the scene — per card a card subscriber and a tag-0 subscriber
on the card row, per deck a name subscriber on the deck row and a date subscriber
on that deck's user row (`APP_SCENE`, :2738-2747) — then, inside
`ctx.binding.frame`, writes a fill label to `APP_FILL_WRITTEN`: the 40 even cards,
decks 0-4 and user 0, 46 rows (:2759-2763). `restore` writes the resting labels
back through `writeAppLabels` (one `patchLabel` per scene row outside `frame`,
one settle, :2805-2808) and unmounts (:2907-2912); `repeatable: false` (:2903);
`auditChurnReads: true` (:2901).

`APP_FILL_WOKE` (:2765) counts the scene mounts whose row was written:
40 card + 40 tag-0 + 5 deck-name + 2 deck-date (decks 0 and 1 read user 0,
`appUserOfDeck`, :2700) = 87.

## What `check` and the oracle prove

`check` (scenarios.ts:2924-2938): one delivery, one distinct render, nothing on
view B, and the line exactly
`${appIds[0]} ${appRanks[0]} ${churnLineOf(87, appReadsOf(filled labels, 1))}`.
`churnLineOf` (render.ts:140-141) is `87:<card 0 label>` on a timed sample and
`87:<card 0 label>#180/<hash>` on the verify pass and the timed process's proof
pass, where `foldChurnReads` (render.ts:124-138) hashes every standing slot's
read by slot index (`setChurnReadsAudited`, worker.ts:489, 644). The oracle
(:2939-2945) writes the same 46 labels and emits the same line; compared in the
verify pass (worker.ts:488-534) and the proof pass (worker.ts:644-662).

The fold names, slot by slot, which label each of the 180 subscribers read. A
subscriber mounted on any other scene row reads that row's label under its own
slot index and changes the hash, so the swap among written (or among unwritten)
rows that a count alone could not see now fails on both audited passes.

## Ways a broken store passes

- **The woke count and the per-slot reads are the adapter's own bookkeeping**:
  `churnWoke` and `churnRead[at]` are set inside the subscriber bodies the
  adapter hands the library (e.g. adapters/redux-toolkit.ts:449-462), and
  `deliverChurn` (render.ts:143-153) folds what the adapter recorded. A body that
  wrote a read the library never delivered would be an adapter defect, outside
  this card.
- **Timed samples carry no fold.** Between the audited passes the line is
  `87:<card 0 label>`; the proof pass runs in the timed process after the
  samples, from the same restored state (worker.ts:644-662).

## Representativeness

Mounting a screen's worth of subscriptions in the same frame as data changes is
what a client does on navigation. Narrow because the data does not arrive (it is
patched), the entities are one collection, and the size is a small screen.

## The standing record, checked (APP_SCRIPT, scenarios.ts:2816-2881)

- A1 MET (:2817-2820) holds: the frame writes rows that mounted subscribers read.
- A2 MET (:2821-2825): `check` fixes deliveries and distinct at one, so the
  redundant count is zero on every passing row.
- A4 MET (:2831-2835): the woke count and the per-slot read fold are compared
  in the timed process's proof pass too (worker.ts:644-662).
- B4 MET (:2849-2855): `appFill` mounts inside the clock and is not in
  `STANDING_FRAME_SCENARIO_KEYS` (floor.ts:69-72), so `stepDeliveryOf` returns
  `mount` (floor.ts:81) and `UNBOUNDED_BECAUSE` declares it (floor.ts:108-119).
- C5 NOT MET (:2872-2880) computes its figures: 46 rows here, 91 per round of
  `appRound`. Agrees with `control-write` declining churn (harness/control.ts:1258).
- B5 (derived): `baseline-array-indexed` declines churn
  (adapters/baseline-array-indexed.ts:405).

card.models: A mounted screen in heavy use: lists of tags growing and shrinking under every card, every deck renamed, every card toggled and one user's setting changed, all in each frame.
card.measures: One frame per round of subscriber mounts or unmounts followed by 91 writes over three entity roles, with the exact number of woken subscribers named in the delivered line.
favours: Stores with cheap mount and unmount: each round mounts 80 tag subscribers, or unmounts 240 on every fourth round (tag count cycles 2, 3, 4, 1 via `appTagsAfter`, scenarios.ts:2701, 2972-2978).

Stores whose wake cost is per subscriber of the written row rather than per standing subscriber. A store with one store-wide listener runs every subscriber's selector at each notification (adapters/redux-toolkit.ts:449-462). Inside `frame` the Redux Toolkit adapter defers notification to the frame end with autoBatch (adapters/redux-toolkit.ts:72-101), so that is one walk over the 180 to 420 standing subscribers per round, not one per dispatch.
Libraries whose batching API `frame` reaches (scenarios.ts:2982-2993) notify once per round instead of 91 times.
biases: Intensity: every card and every deck is rewritten in every one of 20 frames and every card's tag list changes every frame. A real screen does each of these sometimes; all of them every frame is a stress composite.
Single collection, harness-resolved relations, two subscribers per card row at rest: the same scene as `appFill` (see that card).

SELECTIVITY IS ENFORCED, NOT MEASURED. The oracle's line names `appRoundWoke(round)` (scenarios.ts:2702-2703, 3013), so a library that wakes bodies outside the written rows fails rather than ranking slow. Every passing row reports the same counts; time is the only discriminator.
Mounts and unmounts happen before `frame` is opened (scenarios.ts:2973-2978 against :2982), so a library that would batch subscription changes with writes cannot.
card.summary: A dense composite frame — mounts, unmounts and writes over the whole scene, every frame — with an exact wake count and, on audited passes, a per-slot read fold that catch leaked, missing or misplaced subscriptions; real in kind, heavier than any screen sustains.
card.body:
## What the script does

`APP_ROUNDS` = 20 rounds (dataset.ts:177) over the scene mounted and primed in
`prepare` (`prepareStandingAppScene`, scenarios.ts:2964, 2811-2814). Each round
adjusts every card's tag subscribers to `appTagsAfter(round)`, then inside
`ctx.binding.frame` writes a new name to each of 10 decks, a toggled mark to each
of 80 cards and a new setting to user `round % 5`, and settles (:2968-2996). Deck
names are unique per round and card marks alternate between two sets
(:2710-2717), so every write is a change. The run ends with one tag per card
standing (`appTagsAfter(19)` = 1), where it started. `auditChurnReads: true`
(:2961).

## What `check` and the oracle prove

`check` (scenarios.ts:2997-3000): 20 deliveries, 20 distinct renders, nothing on
view B. It does not compare the line itself; the oracle's line per round
(:3001-3015, `emitAppLine` at :2776-2785) names `80·(1 + tags) + 10 + 2` woken
bodies, card 0's mark and, on audited passes, the fold of every standing slot's
read (`appReadsOf`, :2767-2774, which includes the tag slots standing that round;
`churnLineOf`, render.ts:140-141). The digest is compared in the verify pass
(worker.ts:488-534) and in the timed process's proof pass (worker.ts:644-662).

## Ways a broken store passes

- **The woke count and the per-slot reads are the adapter's own bookkeeping**
  (`churnWoke`, `churnRead[at]`, e.g. adapters/redux-toolkit.ts:449-462). The
  fold closes what the previous card listed as passes — a card, tag or deck-name
  subscriber mounted on another row of the same role, and deck-name or date
  subscribers reading a stale value — because each slot's read is hashed under
  its own index.
- **Timed samples carry no fold** (render.ts:115-116); only the two audited
  passes do.
- The stored values are also covered by the population audit (worker.ts:462).

## Representativeness

Mounts, unmounts and writes to several entity roles in one frame is what an
interactive screen produces, and it is the only script here where a frame mixes
subscription changes with data changes at scale. The frequency is not realistic:
read the row as a ceiling on a busy frame.

## The standing record, checked (APP_SCRIPT, scenarios.ts:2816-2881)

- A2's redundant count is fixed at zero by `check`.
- B2's falsifier names the four-to-one tag shrink (:2841-2844), where the anchor's
  `indexOf` plus `splice` unmount is exercised (adapters/baseline-array.ts:638-650).
- B4 MET (:2849-2855): this script mounts inside the clock, so `stepDeliveryOf`
  returns `mount` (floor.ts:81; it is not in `STANDING_FRAME_SCENARIO_KEYS`,
  floor.ts:69-72), and the `mount` reason in `UNBOUNDED_BECAUSE` applies
  (floor.ts:108-119).
- C5 NOT MET (:2872-2880) states 91 writes per round, which matches
  `APP_DECKS + APP_CARDS + 1`.

card.models: A user changes one preference on a mounted screen (date format, locale, a toggle), and only the few components that read it should update.
card.measures: The cost of finding and running the 2 subscribers of one written row among 180 standing ones, per write.
favours: Stores with a per-row or per-value subscriber list: the cost of a step does not depend on how many other subscribers stand.

Against stores with one store-wide listener: every subscriber's selector runs on every write (adapters/redux-toolkit.ts:449-462), 180 per step here. Each step is one dispatch outside `frame`, so autoBatch flushes at once (adapters/redux-toolkit.ts:88-90, 103-108).
biases: On a timed sample the delivered line is the same on every step: woke = 2 and subscriber 0's read, which is card 0 and is never written (scenarios.ts:3038-3046; render.ts:140-141). The moved dates enter the line only on the verify and proof passes, through the per-slot read fold.

The counters the report prints come from the audited passes (verify emit, worker.ts:545-549; proof-pass emit, worker.ts:671-676), where the fold makes every step's line distinct: `check` then expects 20 deliveries and 20 distinct (scenarios.ts:3047-3055), so redundant is 0 on every passing row. The counters are identical across passing rows; only the time differs.
180 standing subscribers is a small screen; the gap between selective and store-wide designs grows with that count, and this point is where it is smallest.
One write per frame, so `frame` is not used and has nothing to change.
card.summary: A common, selective write on a mounted screen; it prices finding a few subscribers among many, its counters are fixed by the check, and the audited fold proves which two bodies ran and what they read.
card.body:
## What the script does

`APP_SETTING_STEPS` = 20 steps (dataset.ts:178) over the scene mounted and primed
in `prepare` (`prepareStandingAppScene`, scenarios.ts:3034, 2811-2814). Each step
writes one user row — user `step % 5`, so each user four times — and settles
(:3038-3046). Only that user's two deck-date subscribers read it
(`APP_DATES_PER_USER`, :2697). `auditChurnReads: true` (:3031).

## What `check` and the oracle prove

`appSettingLinesOf` (scenarios.ts:2795-2803) computes each step's line as
`churnLineOf(2, appReadsOf(labels, 1))`. `check` (:3047-3055) demands 20
deliveries, a distinct count equal to the number of changes between consecutive
computed lines, and nothing on view B. The oracle (:3056-3064) emits those same
lines.

On the verify and proof passes the fold (render.ts:124-138) carries the two date
subscribers' new reads, so every line differs and `check` expects 20 distinct.
That proves, slot by slot, that the two subscribers of the written user — and no
others — read the new value. A store that woke two date subscribers of a different
user, or read a stale value, changes the hash and fails.

## Ways a broken store passes

- **The woke count and the per-slot reads are the adapter's own bookkeeping**
  (`churnWoke`, `churnRead[at]`, e.g. adapters/redux-toolkit.ts:449-462).
- **Timed samples carry no fold**; the proof is the pass after the samples in
  the same process (worker.ts:644-662).

## Representativeness

Changing one setting that a handful of components read, while many others are
mounted, is among the most frequent writes in a client application, and it is
where subscription granularity matters most. The realistic shape, at a small
screen size.

## The standing record, checked (APP_SCRIPT, scenarios.ts:2816-2881)

- A2 MET (:2821-2825) says that on a timed sample this row is distinct once by
  construction, "so the redundant count is that row's whole answer". The
  redundant count the report prints is taken on the audited passes
  (worker.ts:545-549, 671-676), where the same text says every step is distinct,
  so the printed count is 0 on every passing row and carries no answer. The
  falsifier's premise (the timed line) and the counter it points at (the
  audited one) are taken on different passes.
- B4 MET (:2849-2855): this script is in `STANDING_FRAME_SCENARIO_KEYS`
  (floor.ts:69-72), so `stepDeliveryOf` returns `frame` (floor.ts:80) and the
  `frame` reason in `UNBOUNDED_BECAUSE` (floor.ts:120-128) is printed: a step
  mounts nothing and is one write, the bodies that read it, and one line. That
  describes this script.

card.models: Rendering a list from an array of ids against a normalised store: for each id, fetch the entity and render three of its fields. Eight pages of 32 ids, strided through 10,000 rows.
card.measures: The store's key-to-entity lookup and field reads, untracked, plus one 32-line delivery per page; nothing is written and nothing settles.
favours: Stores whose lookup is one hash probe returning a plain object (Map-backed stores; both anchors do one `byId.get` per key, `adapters/baseline-array.ts:357-365`, `adapters/baseline-array-indexed.ts:334-342`) over stores that return proxies, enrich rows, or allocate per read. tanstack-db's keyed read is `collection.get` on the backing collection (`adapters/tanstack-db.ts:830-838`), which returns the row through `getWithVirtualProps` (`node_modules/@tanstack/db/dist/esm/collection/index.js:339-341`, `state.js:137-163`): a virtual-props record per call and an enriched copy cached per key.
TinyBase is read as two `getCell` calls per key and a fresh row object per key (`adapters/tinybase.ts:907-924`); that is the adapter's reading of the library's cell API, not the script's.
biases: The read happens outside any tracking context. In an application the same read occurs inside a component render or a computed and registers a dependency; signal and proxy stores pay that tracking cost there and do not pay it here. Toward fine-grained reactive stores relative to how they would fare on a tracked read.

The ban on resolving keys before the clock (`types.ts:141-143`, `scenarios.ts:4299-4303`) is a rule in prose; no check detects an adapter that kept handles from bind time. Compliance of all adapters is unverified by this card (oimdb `adapters/oimdb.ts:852-860`, mobx `adapters/mobx.ts:578-586`, tanstack-db, tinybase, lokijs `adapters/lokijs.ts:599-607` and both anchors comply).
A 32-line delivery per page is a large share of a step whose store work is 32 map probes; `consumerFloor` is the floor here (`floor.ts:86, 95`), so the multiple column is the reading to use.
Strided keys (`dataset.ts:902-905`) defeat contiguous layouts; a real id list is often in insertion or sort order, which would favour array-backed stores. Toward hash stores, mildly.
card.summary: Untracked lookup of 32 rows by key per page out of 10,000; it prices raw keyed access and delivery, not the tracked read an application's render performs.
card.body:
## The script

`scenarios.ts:4295-4353`: `READ_PAGES` = 8 (`dataset.ts:194`) steps, each
`read.readKeys(page * WINDOW, WINDOW)` (`:4330-4335`). Keys are a stride over the
population (`dataset.ts:902-905`; at n = 10,000 and 256 keys the stride is 39). `check`
(`:4342-4346`) demands exactly 8 deliveries and 8 distinct states of 32 rows on view A and
zero DELIVERIES on view B; `oracle` reads the same keys out of its own Map (`:4347-4352`,
`oracle.ts:379-388`), rendering a missing key as an empty line so a lost row fails rather than
shortens.

## Representativeness

Fetching entities by id is among the most frequent store reads in a front-end, and 32 is a
plausible visible-page size. The narrowing is that the read is a bare pull: no subscription is
formed, so what most reactive stores spend on a read in practice (dependency registration) is
absent. js-framework-benchmark has no store-level equivalent; js-reactivity-benchmark measures
signal reads only inside computations. This row is useful as a raw-access baseline and should
not be read as "render cost of a list".

## Standing (READ_SCRIPT, `scenarios.ts:315-386`)

- A1 MET (`:316-322`) depends on the no-pre-resolution rule, which nothing enforces in code
  (see biases).
- A2 MET (`:323-327`) speaks of "the scroll waking view B" — that is scrollWindow's property;
  for this script `check` demands zero deliveries on view B (`:4346`), so no redundant count
  can arise and a wake there is a failure.
- A4 MET (`:333-337`) holds here: this script does assert an exact delivery count (`:4343`).
- B2 MET (`:343-346`) holds: both anchors do one `Map.get` per key.
- B3 MET (`:347-351`): no adapter declines `reads.byKey`. tanstack-db's plain row declines
  `reads.byWindow` while supplying this shape (`adapters/tanstack-db.ts:1386-1389`), which is
  the per-shape declaration the item describes; its falsifier names "a second library admitted
  that can answer one read shape and not another", and whether that row is what it means is
  not settled by the code.
- C5 NOT MET (`:375-385`) holds: `control-write` declines every read shape
  (`harness/control.ts:1265-1271`).

card.models: A user scrolling a sorted, filtered list: the visible window moves over unchanged data while a second view on the same group stays put.
card.measures: The cost of re-answering a window at a new offset over a maintained or re-derived ordering, plus whatever re-pointing of per-row subscriptions the store does, and whether the unmoved view is woken.
favours: Rescanning stores, for which a new offset is nearly free on top of a scan they do anyway (the lean anchor's `render` walks the population each settle, `adapters/baseline-array.ts:286-301`), and listener-parameterised windows (TinyBase re-registers with offset/limit, `adapters/tinybase.ts:849-862`; `WHY-EACH-ROW.md:2043-2046`).
Stores with change routing that leave view B unwoken (LokiJS dirties neither view on a scroll and re-reads only view A's slice, `adapters/lokijs.ts:608-628`; `WHY-EACH-ROW.md:2047-2049`).
biases: Offsets go 8, 16, 24, 32, 24, 16, 8, 0 at WINDOW 32 (`dataset.ts:877-883`): never deeper than one window into a 200-row group. The deep case is now its own row, `deepScroll` (`scenarios.ts:4415-4457`), whose offsets go out to the group size less one window in four strides (`dataset.ts:884-887`); read this row beside it.
Each step jumps a quarter of the window at once; real scrolling delivers many small offset changes per second. The direction of that bias is unverified.

The comment that group A 'holds only two windows' (`dataset.ts:196-202`) is true at the `small` point (3,200 rows, 64 per group) and not at the default (10,000 rows, 200 per group, `cells/points.ts:4-6`).

oimdb re-points all 32 per-row subscriptions every step: `scrollTo` sets `shapeMoved` (`adapters/oimdb.ts:864-869`) and the next frame's `resync` disposes and re-creates one effect per visible row (`:765-781`), where only 8 rows actually enter and leave. That is the adapter's choice, not the script's, and it counts against oimdb. Its offset is an index into the ordered slot array (`slots[at]` from `state.offset`, `:770-771`), not a prefix walk.

tanstack-db's plain row declines `reads.byWindow` (`adapters/tanstack-db.ts:1386-1389`, reason at `:1368-1374`, an unindexed `setWindow` returns a promise), so this table holds seventeen of the eighteen participants; the eager and indexed tanstack-db rows carry it.
card.summary: Moves a window by a quarter-window up to one window deep and back; prices shallow offset changes only, and is read beside deepScroll, which asks the deep case.

## The script

`scenarios.ts:4355-4413`: `SCROLL_STEPS` = 8 (`dataset.ts:203`) steps of
`read.scrollTo(offset)` + `settle` (`:4393-4400`). Offsets from `dataset.ts:877-883`. `check`
(`:4401-4408`) demands 8 distinct states and a full window on view A, zero distinct states on
view B; redundant deliveries to either view are allowed and reported. View B is the two-axis
window over group A at offset 0 (`oracle.ts:360-363`). `scrollTo` must not re-sort and marks
rather than delivers (`types.ts:144-146`).

## What decides the row

How a store derives "rows `offset .. offset+window` of a group in rank order" without the data
changing. A store that keeps an ordered bucket indexes into it; one that rescans selects
top-(offset + window) from the population (`adapters/baseline-array.ts:287-293`, `visibleInto(...,
offset + view.window)`); TinyBase re-registers a listener; tanstack-db's indexed rows move their
own top-K window with `setWindow` (`adapters/tanstack-db.ts:841-850`). At offsets up to 32 these
differ little.

## Representativeness

Scrolling a virtualised list is one of the most frequent interactions in a data-heavy front
end, so the act is representative. The geometry is shallow: the window never goes deeper than
one window, and the list is a 200-row group. js-framework-benchmark has no scroll test; this is a
genuine addition, and the depth its own comment describes (`scenarios.ts:4363-4368`) is asked by
`deepScroll`.

## Standing (READ_SCRIPT, `scenarios.ts:315-386`)

- A2 MET (`:323-327`) holds: view B's redundant deliveries are the routing signal.
- A4 MET (`:333-337`) says "the exact delivery count these scripts assert"; this script asserts
  distinct counts, not delivery counts (`:4401-4408`).
- B1/B2 MET (`:338-346`) hold for the anchors read: the lean anchor rescans, the indexed one
  selects from the group's bucket (`adapters/baseline-array-indexed.ts:254-268`).
- B3 MET (`:347-351`): tanstack-db's plain row is a library admitted that answers some read
  shapes and declines this one; the falsifier text names exactly that case, and whether it was
  meant to fire on a declined shape is not settled by the code.

card.models: Jumping a virtualised list far from its head and back, as a scrollbar drag does, over data that does not change.
card.measures: How the cost of producing one window grows with its offset into an ordered group, from 42 to 168 rows deep and back, with nothing written.
favours: Stores that keep each group's order as a sequence they can slice at an offset: the deep window costs what the shallow one does.

Against top-k re-selection whose k is offset plus window: both anchors select the top `offset + WINDOW` rows and render the tail (adapters/baseline-array.ts:286-294; adapters/baseline-array-indexed.ts:254-261), as does the mobx view (adapters/mobx.ts:478-488). At the deepest offset k equals the whole 200-row group, so the selection becomes a full insertion sort of the group.

Stores that subscribe per visible row pay one re-point per visible row per step whatever the offset (adapters/oimdb.ts:864-869 sets `shapeMoved`, consumed at :809-810), so depth is not what separates them.
biases: DEEP IS SHALLOW. At the default point a group holds 200 rows (DEFAULT_N 10 000, registry.ts:170; GROUPS 50, dataset.ts:37), so the deepest offset is 168 (`deepStride` = floor((200 − 32) / 4) = 42, dataset.ts:884-887). A virtual list in an application can be thousands of rows deep; the gap between an indexed slice and a growing top-k is smallest here.
Each step jumps 42 rows, not a smooth scroll of a few rows; a store that reuses most of the previous window gets nothing for it.

The description says the deepest offset is the group's size less one window (scenarios.ts:4420-4421). That holds only when `groupSize − WINDOW` is divisible by 4, which it is at the default point (168).
View B, the fixed two-axis window over group A, must not change; the lean anchor re-renders it on every settle (adapters/baseline-array.ts:295-300), counted as redundant and permitted.

`tanstack-db` (autoIndex off) declines `reads.byWindow` (adapters/tanstack-db.ts:1368-1374, 1388): in @tanstack/db 0.15 `setWindow` without an index settles asynchronously. The library is in this table only through `tanstack-db-eager` and `tanstack-db-indexed`, so its unindexed configuration is not priced here.
card.summary: The scroll script at deep offsets, which separates a maintained order from a re-selection that grows with the offset; at the default size the deepest window is only 168 rows in.
card.body:
## What the script does

`SCROLL_STEPS` = 8 (dataset.ts:203). Offsets are `deepStride · (step + 1)` out
and `deepStride · (7 − step)` back (dataset.ts:884-887): 42, 84, 126, 168, 126,
84, 42, 0 at the default point. Each step calls `scrollTo(offset)` and settles
(scenarios.ts:4437-4444). `restore` scrolls to 0 (:4433-4436). Consecutive
offsets differ, including the last of one run (0) against the first of the next
(42).

## What `check` and the oracle prove

`check` (scenarios.ts:4445-4452): view A distinct renders = 8, final view A row
count = `WINDOW`, view B distinct 0. The oracle emits `windowAt(groupA, offset)`
(filter, sort, slice; oracle.ts:287-298) and the axis window per step
(`emitReadViews`, scenarios.ts:4453-4456, oracle.ts:360-363). The digest folds row
counts (consumer.ts:124-127), so a short page at a deep offset fails; it is
compared in both passes (worker.ts:488-531, 644-660).

## Ways a broken store passes

- **The final row count is taken at offset 0.** That every intermediate page is
  full is proved by the digest, not by `check`.
- **Deliveries are not counted**, only distinct renders: a store that delivers
  twice per scroll passes, and its redundant count is printed.
- **A window kept from an earlier sample** at the same offset renders identical
  text; the offsets repeat every run. READ_SCRIPT A1 forbids an adapter doing
  this (scenarios.ts:316-322); `check` cannot see it.

## Representativeness

Virtual scrolling over a sorted list is common, and the question this row asks
(does the window cost grow with its depth) is the one that separates an index
from a rescan. At 200 rows per group it is asked at a small depth. Narrow: read
beside `scrollWindow`, which stays in the first two windows.

## The standing record, checked (READ_SCRIPT, scenarios.ts:315-386, signed at :315)

- A2 MET (:323-327): view B is redundant by construction, holds.
- B4 MET (:352-356): a scroll step delivers one window and `consumerFloor`
  divides the table (`read` is not a flag `stepDeliveryOf` reads, so the shape is
  `window`, floor.ts:76-87, 95). Holds.
- C5 NOT MET (:375-385): "four of the five read scripts perform no store
  mutation" matches `readByKey`, `scrollWindow`, `deepScroll` and `viewSwitch`
  against `filterTwoAxes`.

card.models: A user switching tab or filter: the list view re-points to a different group of already-loaded rows and shows its first page.
card.measures: The cost of changing what a mounted view selects on, with no data written: reading another group's ordered first window and delivering it, eight times.
favours: Stores that keep every group indexed and ordered at write time (a bucket per group plus an ordered list), so a switch reads an existing structure. Both anchors are present for this: the lean anchor rescans the whole population (adapters/baseline-array.ts:286-294, 373-377), the indexed one re-selects from the new group's unordered bucket (adapters/baseline-array-indexed.ts:254-262, 351-355).

Against stores whose view is a query object fixed at construction: TanStack DB builds a new live query per switch (adapters/tanstack-db.ts:850-856), TinyBase re-runs a parameterised query (adapters/tinybase.ts:930-934), LokiJS replaces the DynamicView's filter (adapters/lokijs.ts:615-619). That is how those libraries are used, so the cost is theirs.

Against stores that subscribe per visible row and must re-point every subscription on a switch (oimdb's view holds the new group's bucket and order and releases the old ones per switch, then re-points its per-row effects, adapters/oimdb.ts:871-884, 765-781).
biases: THE SAME SEVEN GROUPS EVERY RUN. `switchGroups` is fixed by the plan (dataset.ts:889-899): g2, g8, g14, g20, g26, g32, g38, then g0 at the default 50 groups. Each timed sample revisits them, so any per-group result a library keeps alive across switches is warm from the second sample on. Whether any library here does so was not checked; the standing forbids it for adapters (A1, B3, scenarios.ts:4473-4477, 4502-4506) and nothing in `check` can see it.

Nothing is written and every group is already resident and of equal size (about 200 rows, dataset.ts:434-454, guard at :759-770). A real switch often coincides with a fetch; this is the in-memory half.
Every switch lands at offset 0 (`TReadBinding.switchGroup`, types.ts:147-149). A switch that keeps a scroll position is not asked.

View B is fixed over group A on the second axis (oracle.ts:360-363). Its silence is free for every store that does not re-run all views on any change; both anchors re-render B on every settle (adapters/baseline-array.ts:295-300; adapters/baseline-array-indexed.ts:263-268) and pay it as redundant deliveries, which `check` permits.
card.summary: A tab or filter switch over resident data; it prices re-selection on a moving view definition, and a library that kept per-group results warm across the fixed sequence would pass unseen.
