## What the script does

`SWITCH_STEPS` = 8 (dataset.ts:205). Each step calls `switchGroup(group)` on the
read binding and settles (scenarios.ts:4543-4550). `switchStride` =
floor(48 / 7) = 6, so the groups are `GROUP_NAMES[2 + 6i]` for i < 7 and then
group A (dataset.ts:889-899); no group repeats and none is a watched group until
the return. `restore` switches back to group A (scenarios.ts:4539-4542), so a run
ends where it began.

## What `check` and the oracle prove

`check` (scenarios.ts:4551-4554): view A distinct renders = 8, the final view A
row count = `WINDOW`, view B distinct = 0. The oracle sends
`windowOf(group)` — filter, sort, slice, independent of `visibleInto`
(oracle.ts:266-276) — to view A once per step (scenarios.ts:4555-4558), and the
digest is compared in both passes (worker.ts:515-530 in verify, 647-656 in the
timed process's proof pass). A wrong group, a short window or an intermediate state
(an empty initial query result, say) changes the digest or the distinct count.

## Ways a broken store passes

- **A cached answer.** A window kept per group from earlier samples renders the
  identical text. The digest cannot distinguish "asked the store" from "kept the
  answer"; only the adapter cards can.
- **Deliveries to view A are not counted**, only distinct renders. A store that
  delivered the same window twice per switch passes; that is permitted and
  printed.
- The final row count is read at group A only; intermediate windows' fullness is
  proved by the digest, not by `check`.

## Representativeness

Switching tabs or filters over loaded data is among the most common view changes
in a client, at roughly this size (10 000 rows, 50 groups, a 32-row page). The
fixed revisiting sequence is the one construction that could flatter a caching
library.

## The standing record, checked (own record, scenarios.ts:4472-4533)

- A1 and B3 MET (:4473-4477, :4502-4506) are promises about adapters; nothing in
  the script enforces them (see biases).
- B4 MET (:4507-4510): `stepDeliveryOf` returns `window` (floor.ts:86) and
  `consumerFloor` divides the table (floor.ts:95). Each step delivers one full
  window, so the floor is a bound on it.
- C5 NOT MET (:4527-4532) agrees with `control-write` declining every read shape
  (control.ts:1265-1271).
- No participant declines `reads.bySwitch`: `readShapes` declines a shape only when
  given a reason (types.ts:170-182), and the one adapter that passes one,
  tanstack-db's plain row, declines `byWindow` only (adapters/tanstack-db.ts:1386-1389).
  So all 18 registered adapters (registry.ts:32-51) have a row.

card.models: Two list views over the same group, one filtered by group alone and one by group AND a second attribute (status AND assignee); rows move between groups and only some of the moves are visible to the narrower view.
card.measures: How often the two-predicate view is woken by a group move of a row its second predicate already excludes, and the cost of four group moves through both views.
favours: Stores that can keep a second index keyed on both predicates, e.g. oimdb's second `OIMIndex` whose `keyOf` folds the axis into the key (adapters/oimdb.ts:692-698, `keyOf` at :694) or LokiJS's `applyWhere` dynamic view (adapters/lokijs.ts:499, 526); such a view is never woken by an off-axis row, by construction.

Because the second axis is derived from the id (`onSecondAxis`, dataset.ts:393-394), any store may file a row on it once at insert and never maintain it; designs with expensive index maintenance pay nothing for the second index here.
biases: The second axis is immutable (dataset.ts:381-392; A1 NOT MET at scenarios.ts:4598-4607): no step changes it, so re-filing a row because the second predicate's field changed is never measured. Toward index-per-predicate designs, whose maintenance cost on that field is exactly what is skipped.

The filter parameters never change: no step switches the view to a different value of either predicate (the user changing a filter chip), which is the most frequent two-axis event in a UI and where a pre-built composite index has to be rebuilt or a second one held. Toward pre-indexed designs. `viewSwitch` (`reads.bySwitch`) switches the group of view A only, never the two-axis view.

Four steps (`steps: 4`, scenarios.ts:4665) and two moved rows; the time is dominated by four settles and up to eight window deliveries. The row's own description says the redundancy count, not the time, is the result (scenarios.ts:4584).

Both movers are the first on-axis and first off-axis rows of view A's window (dataset.ts:862-863), so every move is visible to view A; a move of a row outside both windows (the common case in a 10,000-row store) is not asked here.
card.summary: Counts how often a two-predicate view is woken by moves its second predicate excludes, over four moves; the second predicate is immutable and its parameters fixed, so the hard half of multi-axis filtering is absent.
card.body:
## The script

scenarios.ts:4561-4712: two group moves out to group B and two back (:4677-4688), each
followed by `settle`; `restore` puts both movers back in group A (:4672-4676). View A selects
on group, view B on group and `onSecondAxis(id)`; both over group A (`emitReadViews`,
oracle.ts:360-363). `check` (:4695-4699) demands 4 distinct states on A, exactly 2 on B, a full
window on A; redundant wakes of B are allowed and reported. View B's row count comes from the
plan (`axisWindowSize`, dataset.ts:1102) because the axis halves the group.

## What decides the row

Whether view B's derivation is reached at all by a write to a row its second predicate rejects.
A rescanning store with one dirty flag wakes both views on every step (adapters/baseline-array.ts:286-301,
`render` delivers both pages each settle), giving two redundant deliveries to B; a store with a
composite index files the off-axis mover under a key nobody holds (adapters/oimdb.ts:656, 676-677,
694).

## Representativeness

Two-predicate filtered lists are everywhere in applications (status + owner, folder + unread).
The script is a narrow slice: it moves the FIRST axis and keeps the second immutable and the
predicate values constant. Neither js-reactivity-benchmark nor js-framework-benchmark measures
filtered collections at all; the suite is stronger in having the row and in counting redundant
wakes (consumer.ts:128-133), weaker in that the row cannot tell a store that maintains a
mutable composite index cheaply from one that cannot.

## Standing (own record, scenarios.ts:4597-4664)

- A1 NOT MET (:4598-4607) is accurate. Its count ("all seventeen adapters and the three
  controls") disagrees with the comment above the script ("all eighteen adapters, including
  the sixteen with no row here", :4573-4574); `ADAPTERS` lists eighteen (registry.ts:32-51), and
  no adapter declines `reads.byTwoAxes` (the only decline path is `readShapes`' `declined` map,
  types.ts:170-181, and no adapter passes `byTwoAxes` to it), so "sixteen with no row here" is
  stale.
- A3 MET (:4613-4617) holds: the population audit shows both movers returned.
- B3 MET (:4632-4637) lists the libraries' own predicate mechanisms; checked for oimdb and
  LokiJS only.

card.models: Nothing an application does: the two relation scripts with the store removed, delivering 8-line views straight from arrays of strings.
card.measures: The cost every relation participant pays alike: writing a name or mark into a prepared text array and one `deliverRelation` of 8 lines per step, 16 steps.
favours: Nothing by construction: no participant runs in this table. It divides relationWrite and compositeKeyWrite (`floor.ts:98`, via `stepDeliveryOf` returning `relation` at `floor.ts:82`).
biases: The floor delivers ONE view per step; a participant that wakes both views (the lean anchor, by design: `adapters/baseline-array.ts` relation `settle` renders both on any write) pays two deliveries per step, so its multiple includes a redundant delivery the floor does not. That is intended, and makes every multiple an over-estimate of store work.
The owner-to-lines mapping is computed in `prepare` (`scenarios.ts:5146-5158`), as the adapters do in `holdRelation`; the floor and the participants are on the same footing about the join.

The mark half allocates a template string per step (`scenarios.ts:5184`), as the participants' script does (`scenarios.ts:5005`); both sides carry it. The name half writes prepared strings (`RELATION_NAMES`, `scenarios.ts:4761-4764`), as `relationWrite` does.
card.summary: The delivery-only share of the two relation scripts, measured with no store; a valid divisor for them, not a workload.
card.body:
## The script

`scenarios.ts:5049-5224`: 8 steps write a name into the two lines one owner fills and deliver
view A (`:5175-5180`), then 8 steps write each pair mark and deliver view B (`:5181-5186`).
`steps` = 16 (`:5140`). `check` (`:5188-5191`) demands 8 and 8 distinct states, and 8 lines per
delivery on view B only (`consumers.b.rowCount()`; view A's line count is not asked). The oracle
replays both halves through its own maps and `emitRelation` (`:5201-5223`, `oracle.ts:184`).

## Is it a bound

For the work it contains, yes: every relation participant must at minimum produce the text and
call `deliverRelation`, which this does with array writes and no lookup. Whether any measured
row comes out under it is unverified by this card; `UNBOUNDED_BECAUSE` (`floor.ts:108-119`) names
the mount family as the one whose floor was beaten, and does not say this of relations.

## Standing (own record, `scenarios.ts:5081-5139`)

- B1 MET (`:5103-5107`) holds: no join in the floor.
- B4 MET (`:5115-5118`) holds as far as the code shows (`floor.ts:98`; `standard.ts:472-486`
  checks the step shape of the floor matches the table's).
- C2 MET (`:5123-5126`): its falsifier is this row measured under a different sampling plan from
  the tables it scales; the plan is derived per scenario from that scenario's own probes
  (`cells/runBatch.ts:43-56`), so a different plan is expected. The same note is on the
  `singleFloor` card.
- C5 NOT MET (`:5134-5138`) holds.

card.models: A related record changes and every row showing it updates: a user renames themselves and the 2 messages they authored re-render their author name; repeated for 4 users, 8 times.
card.measures: A write to one entity of a second type reaching a view that renders it against rows of the first type, with the row-to-owner mapping resolved before the clock; plus whether a second view over the same rows (via pair records) is woken.
favours: Stores with per-entity subscriptions on the second type: a subscription on the 4 owner entities wakes view A and never view B (oimdb holds owner slots and row slots at bind, `adapters/oimdb.ts:946` `bindRelationViews`, `holdRelation` from `:1046`, one effect per touched owner slot at `:1074-1080`).

Designs with no relational machinery at all: the foreign key is resolved once by the ADAPTER in `holdRelation` (anchor `adapters/baseline-array.ts:813-834`, `rowOwners`; oimdb `rowOwnerSlots`, `adapters/oimdb.ts:1061-1063`; tanstack-db builds its own `ownerLines` map, `adapters/tanstack-db.ts:1128-1130`, and its owner live query is a `where ... inArray` over the owner collection, not a join, `:1010-1017`), so a store's native join (a live-query join, a relationships module) is neither needed nor credited.
biases: The relationship is immutable (`ownerOf` derives it from the id, `dataset.ts:357-372`; A1 NOT MET at `scenarios.ts:4783-4793`): no step re-parents a row (moving a task to another project), which is where a store's join maintenance is paid. Toward stores without join indexes.

Size is 8 rows, 4 owners, fan-out 2, 8 steps (`dataset.ts:265-287`). A real list of messages with authors is tens to hundreds of rows on screen and thousands in the store; at 8 the delivery and settle constants dominate. Toward stores with low per-frame cost.

Because the join is resolved positionally before the clock, the timed step is one field write on a held owner plus one notification plus an 8-line delivery; it differs from a single-entity column patch mainly in which collection holds the entity.

The lean anchor wakes both views every settle (`adapters/baseline-array.ts:701-708`, one `dirty` flag; `settle` at `:860-865` renders both), so its B deliveries are all redundant by construction; that is the comparison the row is built for, and it counts against the anchor.
card.summary: Eight owner renames reaching an 8-row joined view, with the foreign key resolved by each adapter before the clock; real in shape, tiny in size, and blind to re-parenting and to any store's own join.
card.body:
## The script

`scenarios.ts:4866-4948`: `prepare` calls `holdRelation` once, untimed (`:4901-4903`); each of
`RELATION_STEPS` = 8 steps calls `patchOwnerName(step % 4, name)` and `settle` (`:4914-4920`),
names from `RELATION_NAMES` (`:4761-4764`). `check` (`:4924-4927`) demands 8 distinct states on
view A with 8 rows each and none on view B. The oracle loads owners and pairs into its own maps
and re-derives both views (`:4934-4947`, `oracle.ts:184`). Relation rows are rows `k` and
`100 + k` for `k` < 4, which share an owner by arithmetic (`dataset.ts:992-1017`).

## What decides the row

The cost of a write to a held entity plus routing it to exactly the view that reads it. The
relational step — finding which rows point at the owner — is done by the adapter at bind time
in every binding read for this card (anchor, oimdb, tanstack-db); whether every adapter does the
same is unverified, but `types.ts:198-200` permits it ("the segments are resolved here").

## Representativeness

The event shape (update a parent, children re-render) is among the most common in normalised
front-end state, and few public benchmarks have it: js-framework-benchmark is single-type;
js-reactivity-benchmark has no entity model. So the row covers ground those suites lack. It is
narrow because (a) 8 rows is a toy size, (b) the relationship never moves, and (c) the join is
outside the clock, so a store that answers relations natively and one that does not are timed
on the same notification path.

## Standing (RELATION_SCRIPT, `scenarios.ts:4775-4864`)

- A1 NOT MET is accurate; its text says "the fifteen with no row in these tables at all"
  (`:4791-4792`), but of the eighteen `ADAPTERS` (`harness/registry.ts:32-51`) only
  `baseline-array-indexed` declines `relations` (`adapters/baseline-array-indexed.ts:418-426`);
  seventeen supply a build, and so do all three controls (`harness/control.ts:1186, 1222, 1274`).
  Stale count.
- B1 MET (`:4811-4815`) says the anchor does not work out at bind time that view A depends on
  owners "where the engine is asked to"; in practice every binding read resolves row → owner at
  bind time, the anchor included (`rowOwners`, `adapters/baseline-array.ts:821-823`). The
  asymmetry B1 guards against does not exist, in the other direction from the one it describes.
- B2 MET (`:4816-4819`) says the anchor "rescans"; it renders from pre-resolved arrays
  (`adapters/baseline-array.ts:737-750`) and does not rescan anything.
- C3 MET (`:4846-4849`) says "with two participants"; the tables now hold seventeen
  participants plus the controls.
- The family comment saying `oimdb-3.12.1` is "NOT WIRED for these two scripts"
  (`:4731-4736`) is contradicted by `adapters/oimdb-legacy.ts:1065-1070`, which supplies a
  relation build (adapter name at `:1042`).

card.models: A record that exists per pair of entities (a reaction per (user, message), a read receipt, a membership role per (team, member)) being updated, one pair per frame, while a joined view over the same rows must stay quiet.
card.measures: Composing a two-part key from two identities per call, resolving it to an existing record, writing one field, settling, and delivering an 8-line view; plus whether the joined view is woken.
favours: Stores whose composite lookup is cheap relative to a settle: a joined string into a Map (anchor, `pairKey`, adapters/baseline-array.ts:735, used at :852), a trie over scalar tuples (adapters/oimdb-legacy.ts:747, 766-775, `OIMCollectionStoreTrieDriven`), or a tree over entity slots (adapters/oimdb.ts:946-965, `OIMSlotStoreServiceTreeDriven` in `bindRelationViews`).
Stores that route the pair write to the pair view only; the anchor's single `dirty` flag wakes the joined view redundantly every step.
biases: One key composition per step against one settle and one 8-line delivery per step (scenarios.ts:5004-5007); the composite-key cost the row is named for is likely a small share of each step. That share is unverified by measurement here; `relationFloor` gives the delivery share.

Every record exists before the clock (`holdRelation` in `prepare`, scenarios.ts:4988-4990), so the mint of a new pair (the first reaction on a message) is not measured. Toward stores whose insert path is expensive.

The two key segments are always an existing owner and an existing row; a composite key over scalars that are not entities is out of scope for `@oimdb/core` (scenarios.ts:4725-4729) but measured for `oimdb-3.12.1`, so the table compares two different key shapes under one label, as SCENARIOS.md:158 says.
8 records, 8 steps (`RELATION_ROWS`, dataset.ts:272; `steps`, scenarios.ts:4983): a toy size for a pair table, whose real size is the product of two populations.
card.summary: Eight updates to records keyed by (owner, row), each composed per call; real in kind, but at this size the settle and delivery dominate and minting a pair is not timed.
card.body:
## The script

scenarios.ts:4969-5031: `prepare` calls `holdRelation`, which creates the 8 pair records
(:4988-4990); `restore` writes each back to its seed through the same composed-key path and
resets `pairTurn` (:4993-4999); each run writes all 8 marks in order with a settle after each
(:5000-5008), alternating two disjoint mark sets via `pairTurn` (:5002-5003) so every write is a
change. `check` (:5011-5014) demands 8 distinct states and 8 rows on view B and no distinct
state on view A. The audit reads the key back out of the store (`readPairs`, types.ts:207;
`firstPairMismatch` in `auditStore`, worker.ts:476-481), so a mark in the wrong pair fails even
when it renders right: a real strength of this row.

## Representativeness

Per-pair records are common in applications and are usually modelled as a map keyed by a
joined string. The script is faithful to the update of an existing pair and is the only row in
the suite that times a composed key. It is narrow: 8 records, update only, and a step whose time
is mostly frame and delivery. No public reactivity benchmark has a composite-key case at all.

## Standing (RELATION_SCRIPT, scenarios.ts:4780-4864)

- A1 NOT MET (:4783-4793) concerns the relation being immutable; it applies here only in that
  pair records never change their segments. Its count ("the fifteen with no row in these tables
  at all", :4792) is stale: 15 adapters supply `relations.build` (every adapter file except
  `baseline-array-indexed.ts:418`, which declines; see `relationWrite.md`).
- B3 NOT MET (:4820-4826): one declaration covers both relation scripts. Holds.
- C3 MET text "With two participants" (:4846-4849) is stale for the same reason.
- The description says "this engine ships none" for scalar composite keys (:4979-4981); true
  of `@oimdb/core`, while `oimdb-3.12.1` in the same table keys by scalars
  (adapters/oimdb-legacy.ts:747, 766-775) with `relations.absent: ''` (:1067-1070), contradicting

card.models: Nothing an application does: 32 deliveries of one prepared line through `deliverSingle`, with no store and no value held.
card.measures: The consumer's cost of one single-value delivery, used as the per-step floor for `singleWrite`.
favours: Not applicable: it has one row, measured in one adapter's process (FLOOR_ADAPTER, registry.ts:73), and ranks nobody.
biases: The description calls the bound tight — 'the gap between a row of that family and 1.00 is that row's store and nothing else' (scenarios.ts:5245-5251). The gap also holds the adapter's glue between write and delivery and the harness's `settle` call per step, which this floor does not make. Those belong to using the library, so 'store' should be read as 'store plus its binding'.
The prepared marks are allocated once at module load (SINGLE_MARKS, scenarios.ts:5237-5240) and reused by `singleWrite` (:5427), so neither side allocates a value inside the clock.

It scales `singleWrite` only. `singleResend` sets `rendersNothing` (scenarios.ts:5459), so `stepDeliveryOf` returns `nothing` before it reaches the `single` branch (floor.ts:79, 83) and it has no floor (floor.ts:129-136).
card.summary: An instrument, not a workload: the per-step consumer cost of a one-line delivery, against which `singleWrite` rows are read as multiples.

## What the script does

`run` calls `deliverSingle(consumers.a, name, SINGLE_MARKS[step])` 32 times
(scenarios.ts:5312-5318; render.ts:171-178). `check` demands 32 distinct renders, one
line, and no delivery on view B (:5319-5322). The oracle seeds the two values, emits
them, and sets the named one to each mark in turn (:5323-5332). The floor maps to the
`single` step shape (floor.ts:59) and `BOUND_BY` hands that shape to this floor
(floor.ts:99).

## The standing record, checked (scenarios.ts:5252-5306)

- A3 NOT MET agrees with standard.ts:357-373 (storeless).
- B4 MET (:5282-5285): its falsifier is a single-value row coming out below this
  number. Every passing `singleWrite` step delivers this same line shape, so that holds
  unless an adapter delivers fewer lines than steps, which its `check` refuses
  (scenarios.ts:5431-5434).
- C2 MET (:5290-5293) with falsifier "this row measured under a different sampling plan
  from the single-value tables it scales". The plan is derived per point and per
  scenario from that scenario's own probes (cells/runBatch.ts:43-56; standard.ts:730-732),
  and the repeat count is a function of the median run time (measure.ts:99-138). This
  floor's run is far shorter than a `singleWrite` run, so a different plan is the
  expected outcome, which would make the MET false by its own falsifier. Not verified
  against the runner's output; the same wording is on every floor (scenarios.ts:3186,
  3417, 3625, 3805, 5124).
- C5 NOT MET agrees with the code: storeless (standard.ts:380-397).

card.models: One value the application holds — a toggle, a counter, a selected id — written once per user event and read by one component.
card.measures: The cost of one write to a held value, the library's notification, and a one-line delivery, with a second value beside it that must stay silent.
favours: Libraries built around a value cell with its own subscriber list (signals, atoms): a write is a field store and a short notify.

Against libraries whose every write goes through a collection, document or transaction path; for them this wiring stores one value in machinery made for many. How each adapter maps a single value is the participants' cards' question, not this one's.
biases: One subscriber per value, no derived value, no fan-out: the smallest reactive graph there is. Differences in graph scheduling do not show.
Each step is its own frame, one write and one `settle` (scenarios.ts:5424-5430), so `frame` is not called and has nothing to change.

The bystander is checked for distinct renders only (scenarios.ts:5434); a library that wakes it is counted in its delivery column rather than failed. That is the intended reading (description, scenarios.ts:5409-5411).
card.summary: The commonest write in a signal-style application, sized as it happens — one value, one event, one reader — and checked as a sequence, so a skipped or reordered write fails.
card.body:
## What the script does

`prepare` hands the binding its two values (scenarios.ts:5417-5419); `restore`
writes the resting value back and settles (:5420-5423). The run writes 32
distinct marks (SINGLE_MARKS, :5237-5240), settling after each (:5424-5430).

## What decides correctness

`check` (:5431-5434): 32 distinct renders on view A, one line per delivery, no
distinct render on the bystander. The script is not `finalStateOnly`, so the
sequence digest of both views is compared with the oracle (:5435-5444;
worker.ts:422-439, 515-530, 647-656). The single-value audit reads both values back
through the library and compares them with the model (worker.ts:457-459;
oracle.ts:621-641), which catches a write that landed in the bystander. No case
found where a broken store passes.

## Representativeness

Writing one held value per user interaction is the most frequent write in an
application using signals or atoms, and one reader per value is the typical
shape. Thirty-two steps is a sample size, not a usage claim (dataset.ts:289-305).

## The standing record, checked (SINGLE_SCRIPT, scenarios.ts:5335-5392)

- A1 MET (:5336-5340) holds for this script: every step changes the rendered value.
- A3 MET (:5346-5350) agrees with standard.ts:357-373 (the single branch at :359).
- B4 MET (:5367-5371): scaled by `singleFloor` (floor.ts:83, 99), whose step is the
  same one-line delivery.
- C5 MET (:5388-5391) agrees with the registry: all three controls supply a single
  wiring, `control-write` included (control.ts:1187-1190, 1223-1226, 1286-1289).
- B5 (derived): `baseline-array-indexed` declines the single wiring
  (adapters/baseline-array-indexed.ts:427-436); the other seventeen of the eighteen
  `ADAPTERS` supply it.

card.models: Setting a held value to what it already holds — a state setter called with the current value, a toggle re-applied, a form field re-synced.
card.measures: Whether the library itself suppresses a notification for an unchanged primitive, and the cost of the write path when it does or does not.
favours: Libraries that compare before notifying: they deliver nothing, and a correct row is close to the cost of the write call.
Against libraries that notify on every write: each step wakes the subscriber, which renders the identical line.
biases: The value is a primitive string (`seeds[0]`, scenarios.ts:5467; SINGLE_SEEDS, dataset.ts:328). For a primitive, reference equality is value equality, so any library comparing with `===` or `Object.is` recognises it for free. The row separates 'compares at all' from 'never compares'; it cannot separate structural from reference comparison, which `resendUnchanged` asks with fresh objects (scenarios.ts:1496-1502).

A store whose `writeSingle` does nothing passes: the stored value is `seeds[0]` either way, `check` asks only that nothing distinct was rendered (:5473-5475), and the single-value audit reads back the value the model also holds (worker.ts:457-459; oracle.ts:621-641). `writeSingle` is proved by `singleWrite`, which calls the same method; the proof is across rows, not inside this one.
No floor (`rendersNothing`, :5459; floor.ts:79, 129-136): a row that wakes is not relieved of its consumer share. That is what the row is meant to show.
card.summary: A frequent no-op write, but on a primitive, so it ranks libraries by whether they compare at all; read it beside `singleWrite`, which proves the same write method moves the value.
card.body:
## What the script does

`prepare` hands the binding its two values; `restore` does nothing because
nothing changes (scenarios.ts:5461-5464). The run writes the value already held
32 times, settling after each (:5465-5472). The oracle sets the same value and
emits both views each step (:5476-5485); every emit folds the state already shown,
so the model produces no distinct render.

## Representativeness

Re-applying an unchanged value is common in application code, and frameworks
spend effort bailing out of it (React's `setState` bail-out). For a primitive
held in a signal or atom it is trivial for any library that compares, so the row
is narrow: one corner of change detection, the cheapest one.

## The standing record, checked (SILENT_SINGLE_SCRIPT, scenarios.ts:5394-5401)

- RESOLVED: A1 is now NOT MET (:5396-5400), in a record of its own that spreads
  `SINGLE_SCRIPT` (:5335-5392) and replaces A1 alone, as `SILENT_SCRIPT` does for the
  row family. The previous card's finding — A1 MET contradicting a script whose
  correct answer renders nothing — no longer holds, and `undrivenRowsOf` returns no
  names for this table because it lists rows only when A1 is MET (standard.ts:771-779).
- A2 MET (:5341-5345, inherited) holds: the redundant count is the row's answer here.
- B4 MET (:5367-5371, inherited) holds as written: the falsifier text names this
  script as scaled by no floor, and `UNBOUNDED_BECAUSE` has the `nothing` entry
  (floor.ts:129-136), which standard.ts:451-460 requires.
- C5 MET (:5388-5391, inherited) agrees with the controls: all three supply a single
  wiring (control.ts:1187-1190, 1223-1226, 1286-1289).
